79888.q: Which native willow grows the biggest?
79888.e: The white willow can grow over 25 metres tall. It is the biggest willow in Central Europe.
79888.m: The white willow is the biggest willow here.

79889.q: What can the white willow cope with especially well?
79889.e: White willows grow in floodplains that are often flooded. They survive having their roots under water for weeks.
79889.m: White willows can cope with floods.

79890.q: For which animals are willow flowers an important first food in spring?
79890.e: Willows flower very early in the year. Their flowers give bees their first pollen and nectar after winter.
79890.m: Willows are important for bees in spring.

79891.q: Which continent does the black locust tree come from?
79891.e: The black locust comes from the eastern USA. It was brought to Europe about 400 years ago.
79891.m: The black locust comes from North America.

79892.q: What does the black locust have on its twigs that can prick you?
79892.e: Pairs of sharp thorns grow on the young twigs of the black locust. You have to be careful when you touch them.
79892.m: The black locust has sharp thorns.

79893.q: What do the flowers of the black locust look like?
79893.e: In early summer lots of white flower clusters hang from the black locust. They smell sweet.
79893.m: The black locust has white flower clusters.

79894.q: Which honey usually comes from the black locust?
79894.e: The flowers of the black locust have lots of nectar. The honey made from it is usually sold in shops as acacia honey.
79894.m: Acacia honey usually comes from the black locust.

79895.q: What do the fruits of the black locust look like?
79895.e: The black locust belongs to the legume family, like beans and peas. Its seeds are inside flat, brown pods.
79895.m: The black locust has pods like beans.

79896.q: What is true of the bark and seeds of the black locust?
79896.e: The bark, seeds and leaves of the black locust contain poisonous substances. You must not eat them.
79896.m: The bark and seeds of the black locust are poisonous.

79897.q: What do people like to use the hard wood of the black locust for?
79897.e: Black locust wood is very hard and hardly rots outdoors. That is why posts, fences and playground equipment are made from it.
79897.m: Black locust wood lasts a long time outdoors.

79898.q: How are the leaves of the black locust made up?
a: many small leaflets on one stalk
79898.e: A black locust leaf is made of many small, oval leaflets. They sit on the left and right of a shared stalk.
79898.m: The black locust leaf has many small leaflets.

79899.q: How tall does a field maple usually grow?
79899.e: The field maple is a medium-sized tree. It usually grows 10 to 15 metres tall.
79899.m: A field maple usually grows 10 to 15 metres tall.

79900.q: What do the leaves of the field maple look like?
79900.e: Field maple leaves are only about the size of your palm. They have three to five rounded lobes.
79900.m: The field maple has small leaves with rounded lobes.

79901.q: What colour do field maple leaves turn in autumn?
79901.e: In autumn the field maple turns bright yellow. Sometimes you can also see a little orange.
79901.m: The field maple turns yellow in autumn.

79902.q: What comes out if you break off a leaf stalk of the field maple?
79902.e: White milky sap flows in the leaf stalks of the field maple. This makes it easy to recognise.
79902.m: The leaf stalk of the field maple contains milky sap.

79903.q: Why do people like planting field maples in hedges?
a: It copes well with being cut
It never grows over one metre
79903.e: The field maple keeps sprouting again after being cut. So it forms thick hedges for birds and insects.
79903.m: The field maple copes well with cutting.

79904.q: Which is the smallest of the three common maples in Switzerland?
a: none, they are all the same size
79904.e: The sycamore and the Norway maple grow 20 to 30 metres tall or more. The field maple stays smaller and often grows as a shrub too.
79904.m: The field maple is the smallest native maple.

79905.q: What do the fruits of the field maple look like?
79905.e: The fruits of the field maple have two wings. When they fall, they spin like a little propeller.

79906.q: Where does the field maple like to grow in nature?
a: at the edge of woods and near fields
in the sand by the sea
79906.e: The field maple likes sunny woodland edges and small groups of trees among fields. That is how it got its name.
79906.m: The field maple likes to grow at the edge of woods.

79907.q: When are the leaves of the copper beech most strongly coloured?
a: in spring, when they come out
79907.e: The young leaves of the copper beech glow especially brightly. During the summer they get darker and often a little greenish.
79907.m: Copper beech leaves glow most strongly in spring.

79908.q: Do the seeds of a copper beech always grow into trees with red leaves?
a: No, they all turn out yellow
79908.e: The red leaf colour is not passed on to all the young trees. Both red and green young trees grow from the seeds.
79908.m: Not every young tree from a copper beech has red leaves.

79909.q: What fruits does the copper beech have?
79909.e: The copper beech is a beech with red leaves. Like every beech, it has beechnuts in autumn.
79909.m: The copper beech has beechnuts too.

79910.q: How old can a copper beech get?
79910.e: Beeches live about 200 to 300 years. Many copper beeches in parks were planted over 100 years ago.
79910.m: A copper beech can live over 200 years.

79911.q: Where do you see big copper beeches especially often?
a: In the reeds by a lake
79911.e: Because of its beautiful red leaves, people liked to plant the copper beech in parks. Old trees often stand near castles and villas.

79912.q: Why are the leaves of the copper beech red and not green?
a: A red pigment covers up the green
79912.e: Copper beech leaves have green chlorophyll too. But a red pigment in the outer layer covers it up.
79912.m: In copper beech leaves, red covers up the green.

79913.e: Beechnuts are small nuts with three edges. Usually two of them sit together in one husk.

79914.q: In German the copper beech is called the “blood beech”. Where does this name come from?
79914.e: The leaves of the copper beech are dark red like blood. That is why it is called the blood beech in German.
79914.m: The copper beech has dark red leaves.

80015.q: What do you say about someone who is especially good at making plants grow?
80015.e: “Having green fingers” is a saying. It is said about people who are good with plants.
80015.m: If you have green fingers, you are good at gardening.

80016.q: How many finger bones (sections) does the thumb have?
80016.e: The thumb has only two sections. That is why it is shorter than most of the other fingers.

80017.q: Which finger can touch the tips of all the other fingers on the same hand?
80017.e: You can place your thumb opposite the other fingers. That way you can grip well, for example a pencil or a spoon.
80017.m: With the thumb you can grip well.

80018.q: What does it usually mean when someone gives a thumbs up?
80018.e: A thumbs up is a sign for “good” or “everything's fine” here.

80019.q: What are you wishing someone when you keep your fingers crossed for them?
80019.e: “I'll keep my fingers crossed for you” is a saying. You use it to wish someone lots of luck. In German-speaking countries people press their thumbs instead.
80019.m: Keeping your fingers crossed means wishing luck.

80020.q: Which finger do many babies like to suck?
80020.e: Many babies suck their thumb. It calms them, and some even do it before they are born.

80021.q: What is the name of the tiny girl in Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale who is only as big as a thumb?
80021.e: In the fairy tale “Thumbelina”, a tiny girl has lots of adventures. Her name comes from the word thumb.
80021.m: Thumbelina is only as big as a thumb.

a: A little book of pictures that move when you flick through it
A very small cinema for mice
80022.e: With a flip book you let the pages run quickly past your thumb. The pictures then look as if they are moving.
80022.m: A flip book turns lots of pictures into a little film.

80023.q: What does a hitchhiker at the side of the road show with their thumb?
a: That they would like a lift
That they are showing the way
80023.e: Hitchhikers hold their thumb out in the direction of travel. That way they show drivers that they would like a lift.
80023.m: With their thumb, a hitchhiker shows that they want a lift.

80024.q: Which finger is right next to the thumb?
80024.e: Next to the thumb comes the index finger. It is the second finger of the hand.
80024.m: The index finger is next to the thumb.

80025.q: Which finger do you usually point at something with?
80025.e: The index finger is also called the pointing finger. You use it to point at things or directions.
80025.m: You point at things with your index finger.

80026.q: Which finger do many children stick up at school when they want to answer?
80026.e: If you want to say something, you put up your hand and often stretch your index finger up. That way the teacher can see who wants to speak.
80026.m: When you put your hand up, you often stretch up your index finger.

80027.q: What does someone mean who holds their index finger in front of their lips?
80027.e: The index finger in front of the lips means “shh”. You use it to ask others to be quiet.
80027.m: A finger in front of the lips means “Be quiet!”.

80029.q: What does someone often mean when they raise their index finger while talking?
80029.e: A raised index finger is a warning. It means that someone should be careful or listen.
80029.m: A raised index finger is a warning.

80030.q: How many sections does the index finger have?
80030.e: The index finger has three sections. The middle finger, ring finger and little finger have just as many.
80030.m: The index finger has three sections.

80031.q: Which finger do many children run along under the line when they are learning to read?
80031.e: When you are learning to read, your index finger helps you not to lose your place in the line. You follow along word by word.
80031.m: The index finger helps when you are learning to read.

80032.q: Which finger do you usually press a lift button with?
80032.e: The index finger is skilful and easy to control. That is why you usually press buttons and doorbells with it.
80032.m: You usually press buttons with your index finger.

80033.q: Which finger is the longest for most people?
80033.e: The middle finger is the longest finger for almost everyone. It is in the middle of the hand.
80033.m: The middle finger is the longest finger.

80034.q: Between which two fingers is the middle finger?
80034.e: The middle finger has a neighbour on each side. On one side is the index finger, on the other the ring finger.
80034.m: The middle finger is between the index finger and the ring finger.

80035.q: When playing the piano, each finger has a number, and the thumb is 1. Which number is the middle finger?
80035.e: You count from the thumb: thumb 1, index finger 2, middle finger 3. In piano music these numbers are written above the notes.
80035.m: On the piano, the middle finger is number 3.

80036.q: Which three fingers do people in Switzerland hold up when they swear an oath?
a: Thumb, index finger and middle finger
Index finger, ring finger and little finger
Thumb, ring finger and little finger
Middle finger, ring finger and little finger
80036.e: When swearing an oath, you raise your hand with the thumb, index finger and middle finger. The Rütli oath is often shown this way too.
80036.m: When swearing an oath, you hold up your thumb, index finger and middle finger.

80037.q: On which finger do many schoolchildren get a small hard patch from lots of writing?
80037.e: When you write, the pencil usually rests on the middle finger. The pressure can cause a small hard patch there.
80037.m: When you write, the pencil rests on the middle finger.

80038.q: On which finger do many married people wear their wedding ring?
80038.e: The wedding ring is usually worn on the ring finger. That is where this finger gets its name.
80038.m: You wear your wedding ring on your ring finger.

80039.q: Which finger is between the middle finger and the little finger?
80039.e: If you count from the thumb, the ring finger is the fourth finger. It is next to the little finger.
80039.m: The ring finger is the fourth finger.

80040.q: Which finger is the hardest to move completely on its own?
80040.e: The ring finger is closely connected to its neighbours by tendons. That is why they often move too when you try to straighten it alone.
80040.m: The ring finger is hard to move on its own.

80041.q: For many people, which finger is about the same length as the index finger?
80041.e: For many people, the index finger and ring finger are almost the same length. In some people one is a little longer, in others the other.
80041.m: The ring finger and index finger are often almost the same length.

80042.q: Which finger is the smallest on the hand?
80042.e: The little finger is the shortest and thinnest finger. Its name says it all.
80042.m: The little finger is the smallest finger.

80043.q: Which finger is right on the outside, on the opposite side of the hand from the thumb?
80043.e: The thumb is on one side and the little finger right on the other side. It is the fifth finger.
80043.m: The little finger is the fifth finger.

80044.q: How do many children make a really firm promise to each other?
a: They hook their little fingers together
80044.e: In a pinky promise, two children hook their little fingers together. It counts as an especially firm promise.
80044.m: With hooked little fingers you make a promise.

80045.q: How does the saying continue: “Give him an inch, ...”?
a: and he'll give you a foot
80045.e: The saying means: if you give someone a little, they immediately want much more.
80045.m: Give him an inch and he'll take a mile.

80046.q: In touch typing, which finger do you use to press the Enter key on the right of the keyboard?
80046.e: The Enter key is right on the outside on the right. That is why it is easiest to reach with your right little finger.
80046.m: You press the Enter key with your right little finger.

80047.q: How many little fingers does a person usually have?
80047.e: Each hand has one little finger. With two hands, that makes two.
80047.m: Each hand has one little finger.

80049.q: What is the inside of the hand called?
80049.e: The inside of the hand is called the palm. You use it to hold and grab things.
80049.m: The inside of the hand is called the palm.

80050.q: What never grows on the palm of your hand?
80050.e: The skin of the palm has no hair roots. That is why hair never grows there.
80050.m: No hair grows on the palm.

80051.q: What do you call the creases in the palm of your hand?
80051.e: Every palm has large creases, the palm lines. They help the skin to fold when you grip.
80051.m: The creases in the palm are called palm lines.

80052.q: What often happens to the palms of your hands when you are very nervous?
80052.e: There are very many sweat glands in the palm. When you are nervous, they often sweat and your hands get damp.
80052.m: When you are nervous, your hands often get sweaty.

80053.q: Which parts of your hands do you hit together when you clap?
80053.e: When you clap, your two palms meet. That makes the loud clapping sound.
80053.m: When you clap, you hit your palms together.

80054.q: What is the skin on the palm like compared with the back of the hand?
80054.e: The skin of the palm is thicker and tougher. That way it can cope with lots of rubbing and gripping.
80054.m: The skin of the palm is thick and tough.

80055.q: Which part of the hand is usually lighter than the rest in people with dark skin?
80055.e: The palm has less pigment in the skin. That is why, for many people, it is lighter than the back of the hand.
80055.m: The palm is often lighter than the rest of the hand.

80056.q: What do you call a hand shaped like a little bowl?
80056.e: If you shape your palm into a bowl, you get a cupped hand. You can scoop up water in it, for example.
80056.m: You can carry water in a cupped hand.

80057.q: Which part of your hand is best for catching a ball?
80057.e: The palm is soft and big. The ball lands in it, and the fingers close round it.
80057.m: You catch a ball with your palm.

80058.q: Who has exactly the same fingerprint as you?
80058.e: Every fingerprint is unique. Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
80058.m: Every person has their own fingerprint.

80059.q: Who looks for fingerprints at a crime scene?
80059.e: The police collect fingerprints at the crime scene. That way they can find out who was there.

80060.q: What can you see on a fingerprint?
80060.e: The skin of the fingertip has fine ridges. They form lines that you can see in the print.
80060.m: A fingerprint is made of fine lines.

80061.q: What happens to the pattern of your fingerprint as you get older?
80061.e: The pattern of a fingerprint stays the same for a whole lifetime. As you grow, it just gets bigger.
80061.m: The pattern of a fingerprint always stays the same.

80062.q: Which shape is a typical pattern in fingerprints?
80062.e: In fingerprints, there are mainly arches, loops and whorls. The loop is the most common pattern.
80062.m: Loops, arches and whorls are fingerprint patterns.

80063.q: Which animal has fingerprints that are very similar to human ones?
80063.e: Koalas have fingerprints that can hardly be told apart from human ones. They help them to grip branches.

80064.q: When does a person get their fingerprints?
80064.e: Fingerprints form while the baby is still growing in its mother's tummy. By birth they are finished.

80065.q: What can you use to unlock many mobile phones without typing in a number?
80065.e: Many phones have a sensor that recognises fingerprints. Because every print is different, the phone only opens for its owner.

80066.q: What has been stored on the chip of the Swiss passport since 2010?
80066.e: Since 2010 the Swiss passport has contained a chip. A photo and two fingerprints are stored on it.
80066.m: Two fingerprints are stored in the Swiss passport.

80067.q: How can you make your fingerprint clearly visible on paper?
a: Press your finger on an ink pad
Blow on the paper with your finger
Hold your finger in the sun
80067.e: With ink from an ink pad, the pattern of lines stays visible on the paper. That way you can compare prints.
80067.m: You can make fingerprints with an ink pad.

80068.q: What do your fingers leave behind when you touch a clean drinking glass?
80068.e: The skin gives off a little grease and sweat. That is why fingerprints are left behind on smooth surfaces such as glass.
80068.m: Fingerprints are left behind on glass.

80069.q: What is the soft, round end of a finger called?
80069.e: The fingertip is the soft pad at the front end of the finger. You use it to touch and feel.
80069.m: The end of the finger is called the fingertip.

80070.q: What do blind people use to read Braille?
80070.e: Braille is made of small raised dots. Blind people feel them with their fingertips.
80070.m: You read Braille with your fingertips.

80071.q: Which part of the hand can feel things most finely?
80071.e: There are particularly many nerves in the fingertips. That is why you can feel even tiny differences there.
80071.m: The fingertips feel things especially finely.

80072.q: What do your fingertips look like after a long bath?
80072.e: After a long time in water, the skin on the fingertips gets wrinkles. After drying off, it becomes smooth again.
80072.m: After a bath your fingertips are wrinkly.

80073.q: What do guitar players often get on their fingertips over time?
80073.e: When playing the guitar, the fingertips press hard on the strings. The skin protects itself by forming hard skin.
80073.m: Guitar players often have hard skin on their fingertips.

80074.q: Which part of the finger is best for using a phone screen?
80074.e: A touchscreen reacts to skin. With a hard fingernail it usually does not work.
80074.m: You use a touchscreen with your fingertip.

80075.q: What do you put on your finger when sewing so that the needle does not prick your fingertip?
80075.e: A thimble is a little cap made of metal or plastic. With it you push the needle through the fabric without pricking yourself.
80075.m: A thimble protects your fingertip when sewing.

80076.q: What is on the top of the finger, directly above the fingertip?
80076.e: Underneath, at the end of the finger, is the soft fingertip. Above it sits the hard fingernail, which protects it.
80076.m: The fingernail sits above the fingertip.

80077.e: Fingernails are made of horny cells containing the substance keratin. Hair is made of it too.

80078.q: Why does it not hurt to cut your fingernails?
a: The front of the nail has no nerves
The scissors only press very gently
The skin holds back the pain
80078.e: There are no nerves in the white front part of the nail. That is why you feel no pain when you cut it.
80078.m: The front part of the nail has no nerves.

80079.q: What is the pale curve at the bottom of the fingernail called?
80079.e: At the bottom of the nail you can often see a pale curve. It is called the lunula, which means ‘little moon’, because it looks like a half-moon.
80079.m: The pale curve at the bottom of the nail is called the lunula.

80080.q: Roughly how much does a fingernail grow in a month?
80080.e: Fingernails grow slowly, about half a millimetre to one millimetre a week. In a month that is only a few millimetres.
80080.m: Fingernails only grow a few millimetres a month.

80081.e: The hard nail protects the sensitive fingertip. It also helps you pick up small things.

80082.q: Which grow faster: fingernails or toenails?
80082.e: Fingernails grow faster than toenails. That is why you have to cut them more often.

80083.q: What is the thin skin at the bottom edge of the fingernail called?
80083.e: The cuticle is at the bottom edge of the nail. It protects the place where the nail grows from.
80083.m: The cuticle protects the root of the nail.

80084.q: What is best for cutting fingernails?
80084.e: Nail scissors are small and often have curved blades. With them you can trim your nails neatly.
80084.m: You cut fingernails with nail scissors.

80085.q: What do cats have on their paws where we have fingernails?
80085.e: Cats have sharp claws. They can stick them out and pull them back in.
80085.m: Cats have claws instead of flat nails.

80086.q: How many fingernails does a person usually have?
80086.e: A person has two hands with five fingers each. There is a nail on each finger, so that makes ten.

80087.q: What happens to a fingernail after you have cut it?
80087.e: The nail keeps growing from the nail root. That is why you have to keep cutting your nails.

80088.q: What helps you pick up a coin from a smooth table?
80088.e: With the hard edge of your fingernails you can get under the flat coin. With the soft fingertip alone it is difficult.
80088.m: Fingernails help you pick up small things.

80089.q: What is the outer side of the hand called?
80089.e: The top side of the hand is called the back of the hand. The inside is the palm.
80089.m: The outer side of the hand is called the back of the hand.

80090.q: What can you often see showing through the skin on the back of your hand in a bluish colour?
80090.e: On the back of the hand the skin is thin. That is why you can see the veins as bluish lines.
80090.m: You can often see the veins on the back of your hand.

80091.q: What do you see as little hills on the back of your hand when you make a fist?
80091.e: When you make a fist, your knuckles stick out. They are the joints between the hand and the fingers.
80091.m: When you make a fist, you can see your knuckles.

80092.q: Which side of the hand faces upwards when you lay your hand flat on the table?
80092.e: When you lay your hand flat, the palm lies on the table. On top you then see the back of the hand.
80092.m: When your hand lies flat, the back of the hand is on top.

80093.q: What moves under the skin on the back of your hand when you move your fingers?
80093.e: Tendons connect the muscles in the arm to the fingers. On the back of the hand you can see them as cords when you straighten your fingers.

80094.q: Where on the hand do doctors in hospital often put a needle for a drip?
a: On the back of the hand
80094.e: On the back of the hand, the veins are close under the skin. That is why it is a good place to put in a needle for a drip.
80094.m: Drips are often given through the back of the hand.

80095.q: Where on the hand do fine hairs grow for many people?
a: On the back of the hand
80095.e: There are hair roots on the back of the hand. That is why fine hairs grow there for many people.
80095.m: Fine hairs grow on the back of the hand.

80096.q: What do you call a person who mainly writes with their left hand?
80096.e: If you use your left hand more skilfully, you are a left-hander. Left-handers usually write, draw and throw with their left.
80096.m: If you write with your left hand, you are a left-hander.

80097.q: Roughly how many people are left-handed?
80097.e: It is estimated that about ten per cent of people are left-handed. That is about one person in ten.
80097.m: About one person in ten is left-handed.

80098.q: Which scissors are best for left-handers?
80098.e: On left-handed scissors the blades are arranged the other way round. That way a left-hander can see the line well while cutting.

80099.q: On which day is International Left-Handers Day?
80099.e: International Left-Handers Day is celebrated every year on 13 August. It draws attention to the needs of left-handers.

80100.q: What are left-handed children told today?
a: They may write with their left hand
They must write with their right hand
They may not write at all
They must write with their foot
80100.e: In the past, left-handers were often forced to write with their right hand. Today we know that they should write with their strong left hand.
80100.m: Left-handers may write with their left hand.

80101.q: What can easily happen to left-handers when they write with ink?
80101.e: We write from left to right. So the left hand moves over the fresh ink and can smudge it.
80101.m: Left-handers have to watch out for fresh ink.

80102.q: Can you choose whether you become left-handed?
a: No, you are usually born that way
Yes, you choose at the age of 10
Yes, it is drawn by lot
80102.e: Whether you are left-handed is usually something you are born with. You can already tell in small children.
80102.m: Left-handedness is usually something you are born with.

80103.q: What can you buy specially for left-handers to make writing easier?
80103.e: There are fountain pens with a special nib for left-handers. With them there is less scratching and fewer blots when writing.
80103.m: There are special fountain pens for left-handers.

80104.q: What do you call a person who can use both hands equally well?
80104.e: If you can use both hands equally skilfully, you are ambidextrous. That is quite rare.
80104.m: An ambidextrous person can use both hands equally well.

80105.q: Which half of the brain mainly controls the right hand?
80105.e: The brain controls the sides of the body crosswise. The left half of the brain steers the right side of the body.
80105.m: The left half of the brain controls the right hand.

80106.q: Which hand do people in Switzerland usually shake when greeting each other?
80106.e: When shaking hands in Switzerland, people give each other their right hand. This also applies to left-handers.
80106.m: When greeting, you give your right hand.

80107.q: On which side of the plate does the knife go when laying the table?
80107.e: The knife goes on the right of the plate and the fork on the left. That way it is comfortable for cutting for most people.
80107.m: The knife goes on the right of the plate.

80108.q: How can you often tell whether a small child is right-handed?
a: They mostly grab and draw with their right hand
They have more hair on the right
They sleep on their right side
They have bigger ears on the right
80108.e: Children show their strong hand when they grab, draw and throw. If a child mostly uses the right hand, they are probably right-handed.
80108.m: The hand a child draws with is usually their strong hand.

80109.q: On which side of the keyboard is the computer mouse usually placed for right-handers?
80109.e: Right-handers use the mouse with their right hand. That is why it lies to the right of the keyboard.
80109.m: Right-handers have the mouse on the right.

80110.q: Which hand is usually a little stronger in right-handers?
80110.e: Right-handers use their right hand more often. That is why it is usually a little stronger and more skilful.
80110.m: In right-handers, the right hand is often stronger.

80111.q: Which hand does a right-hander write with?
80111.e: A right-hander uses their right hand for fine work such as writing. It is their skilful hand.
80111.m: Right-handers write with their right hand.

80112.q: Which two fingers do you usually use to click your fingers?
80112.e: To click your fingers, you press your middle finger firmly against your thumb. Then it slips off and hits the base of your hand. That makes the sound.
80112.m: You usually click your fingers with your thumb and middle finger.

80113.q: Which part of the hand do many parents use to check quickly whether a child's forehead is hot?
80113.e: The skin on the back of the hand feels warmth well. That is why many parents put the back of their hand on the forehead when a child seems ill.
80113.m: The back of the hand feels warmth well.

80114.q: How can you tell that a force is acting on an object?
a: It moves differently or changes shape
80114.e: A force can move, slow down, steer or bend an object. That is how you can tell a force is acting.
80114.m: Forces move things or change their shape.

80115.q: Which force turns a waterwheel on a stream?
80115.e: The flowing water pushes against the paddles of the wheel. This makes the waterwheel turn.
80115.m: Flowing water can turn a wheel.

80116.q: Which famous scientist is the unit of force named after?
80116.e: Isaac Newton was an English scientist. He described the laws of motion, which is why the unit of force is named after him.
80116.m: The unit newton is named after Isaac Newton.

80117.q: Which force pulls everything down towards the Earth?
80117.e: The Earth pulls everything towards itself. This force is called gravity.
80117.m: Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth.

80118.q: What is needed for a ball that is lying still to start rolling?
80118.e: A ball that is lying still stays where it is. Only when a force acts on it, for example a kick, does it start to roll.
80118.m: Without a force, a ball lying still stays put.

80119.q: Why does a toy car stop sooner on a carpet than on a smooth floor?
a: The carpet slows it down more
80119.e: There is a lot of friction between the wheels and the carpet. Friction is a force that slows things down.

80120.q: What does the force of the brakes do to a moving bike?
80120.e: The brakes press against the wheel. This force acts against the movement, so the bike slows down.

80121.q: In physics, how do you draw a force?
80121.e: An arrow shows the direction in which the force acts. A long arrow means a large force.
80121.m: A force is drawn as an arrow.

80122.q: Can you see a force with your eyes?
a: Yes, but only in the dark
Yes, if it is very big
80122.e: A force itself is invisible. You only see what it does, for example that something moves or bends.
80122.m: Forces are invisible; you only see their effect.

80123.q: Which force drives a sailing boat?
80123.e: The wind pushes against the sail. This pushes the boat across the water.
80123.m: A sailing boat moves with wind power.

80124.q: What are you doing to a shopping trolley when you move it in front of you?
80124.e: When you move something in front of you, you push it. The force points away from you.
80124.m: What you move in front of you, you push.

80125.q: What do you do to a drawer when you open it?
80125.e: To open a drawer, you pull it towards you. To close it, you push it back again.
80125.m: You open a drawer by pulling.

80126.q: What does a locomotive do with the carriages behind it?
80126.e: The locomotive is at the front and is coupled to the carriages. It pulls them along behind it.

80127.q: What do you have to do with a door that says “Push”?
80127.e: “Push” means you have to press the door away from you. With “Pull” you pull it towards you.
80127.m: You press a door marked “Push” away from you.

80128.q: Which way does the force point when you pull on a rope?
80128.e: When you pull, you bring something towards you. That is why the force points towards yourself.
80128.m: When you pull, the force points towards you.

80129.q: What is the easiest way to move a heavy suitcase with wheels?
a: Pull it along on its wheels
Push it lying on its side
Throw it in front of you
80129.e: The wheels carry the weight of the suitcase. You only have to pull it along behind you.
80129.m: With wheels, a suitcase is easy to pull.

80130.q: What does a snowplough do with the snow on the road?
a: It pushes it to the side
It pulls it along behind it
It throws it into the air
80130.e: The snowplough has a slanted blade at the front. With it, it pushes the snow to the side of the road.
80130.m: A snowplough pushes the snow away.

80131.q: What do you use to pull a cork out of a bottle?
80131.e: You twist the corkscrew into the cork and pull it out. In Switzerland a corkscrew is called a “Zapfenzieher”.
80131.m: You pull out a cork with a corkscrew.

80132.q: What is the game called in which two teams pull on the ends of a rope?
80132.e: In a tug of war, two teams pull in opposite directions.
80132.m: In a tug of war, two teams pull on one rope.

80133.q: When does a team win a tug of war?
a: When it pulls the rope over to its side as far as a mark
When it has the most people
80133.e: There are marks on the ground and on the rope. Whoever pulls the rope far enough over to their side has won.
80133.m: In a tug of war, the team that pulls the rope to its side wins.

80134.q: What happens in a tug of war when both teams pull exactly as hard as each other?
a: The rope flies into the air
80134.e: When both sides pull equally hard, the forces cancel each other out. The rope then stays where it is.
80134.m: Equal forces in opposite directions cancel each other out.

80135.q: At which big games was tug of war a sport from 1900 to 1920?
80135.e: Tug of war was part of the Olympic Games from 1900 to 1920. Today it has its own world championships.
80135.m: Tug of war used to be an Olympic sport.

80136.q: Which shoes are best for a tug of war on grass?
80136.e: In a tug of war, you dig your feet firmly into the ground. Shoes with a tread do not slip.
80136.m: For a tug of war you need shoes with a good grip.

80137.q: How do good tug of war players stand?
a: Leaning back with their feet planted firmly
With their back to the rope
80137.e: If you lean back and dig your feet firmly into the ground, you can put a lot of force on the rope.
80137.m: In a tug of war you dig your feet firmly into the ground.

80138.q: Apart from strength, what is especially important in a tug of war?
a: Everyone pulls at the same time
80138.e: When everyone pulls at the same moment, their forces add up. That is stronger than everyone pulling on their own.
80138.m: In a tug of war it helps if everyone pulls at the same time.

80139.q: In which directions do the two teams pull in a tug of war?
80139.e: Each team pulls the rope towards itself. So the two forces point in opposite directions.
80139.m: In a tug of war, the teams pull against each other.

80140.q: What is the mark in the middle of the rope for?
a: You can see which way the rope is moving
You can hang the rope up by it
80140.e: At the start, the mark is exactly above the centre line. If it moves, you can see which team is pulling harder.
80140.m: The mark on the rope shows who is pulling harder.

80141.q: How many wheels does an ordinary wheelbarrow have?
80141.e: An ordinary wheelbarrow has a single wheel at the front. At the back it has two handles.
80141.m: A wheelbarrow usually has one wheel.

80142.q: What do you use a wheelbarrow for?
a: To carry heavy things like soil
80142.e: In the garden or on a building site, you use a wheelbarrow to carry soil, sand or stones.
80142.m: You use a wheelbarrow to carry heavy things.

80143.q: Why is a heavy load easier to move in a wheelbarrow than in your arms?
a: The wheel carries a large part of the weight
The load gets lighter in the wheelbarrow
The handles are made of rubber
80143.e: A large part of the weight presses down on the wheel. So you only have to hold a small part yourself.
80143.m: With a wheelbarrow, the wheel carries much of the weight.

80144.q: Where should you put a heavy load in a wheelbarrow so that it is easier to lift?
a: As close to the wheel as possible
Right at the back by the handles
80144.e: The closer the load is to the wheel, the less force you need at the handles.
80144.m: Put heavy loads in a wheelbarrow close to the wheel.

80145.q: What is the simple machine called that a wheelbarrow works like?
80145.e: A wheelbarrow is a lever: the wheel is the pivot, and with a small force on the long handles you lift a heavy load.
80145.m: A wheelbarrow works like a lever.

80147.q: What does a wheelbarrow have at the back so that it stands safely?
80147.e: Under the tray at the back, the wheelbarrow has two legs. Together with the wheel, it stands safely on three points.
80147.m: A wheelbarrow stands on its wheel and two legs.

80148.q: What does a sledge glide on over the snow?
80148.e: A sledge has long, smooth rails underneath, called runners. With them it glides over snow and ice.

80149.q: Why does a sledge glide so well on snow?
a: The sledge is lighter than air
80149.e: There is only a little friction between the smooth runners and the snow. That is why the snow hardly slows the sledge down.
80149.m: A sledge glides well on snow because there is little friction.

80150.q: What do you have to do to get a sledge up the slope?
80150.e: To get up the slope, you have to pull the sledge on a string. You need muscle power for this.
80150.m: You pull the sledge up the slope.

80151.q: What is the well-known wooden sledge called that is named after a place in the Grisons?
80151.e: The Davos sledge is a wooden sledge with metal runners. It is named after the town of Davos in the Grisons.
80151.m: The Davos sledge is a well-known Swiss sledge.

80152.q: What do you usually brake with on a simple wooden sledge?
80152.e: A simple wooden sledge has no brake. You brake and steer by putting your feet into the snow.
80152.m: On a wooden sledge you brake with your feet.

80154.q: Which animals often pull sledges over the snow in cold countries?
80154.e: Sled dogs are strong and like to run long distances. They pull sledges in places such as Alaska or Greenland.

80155.q: When does a sledge go down the slope faster?
80155.e: The steeper the slope, the more strongly the Earth pulls the sledge down. That is why it gets faster.
80155.m: On a steep slope the sledge goes faster.

80156.q: What is the racing sledge called in which two or four people race down an ice track?
80156.e: A bobsleigh is a racing sledge with steering and a brake. On the ice track it reaches very high speeds.
80156.m: On the ice track you ride in a bobsleigh.

80157.q: What happens to a stretched rubber band when you let go of it?
80157.e: A rubber band is elastic. After stretching, it goes back to its old shape by itself.
80157.m: A rubber band shrinks back after being stretched.

80158.q: What happens to a rubber band when you pull at both ends?
80158.e: When you pull at both ends, the rubber band stretches. It gets longer and thinner.
80158.m: A rubber band gets longer when you pull it.

80159.q: What do you feel when you stretch a rubber band further and further?
a: It pulls back more and more strongly
It pulls back more and more weakly
80159.e: The further you stretch a rubber band, the more strongly it wants to shrink back. So you need more and more force.
80159.m: The more you stretch rubber, the more strongly it pulls back.

80160.q: What happens if you stretch a rubber band far too much?
80160.e: Every rubber band only holds up to a certain length. If you stretch it further, it snaps.
80160.m: Stretched too far, a rubber band snaps.

80161.q: The sap of which tree is used to make natural rubber?
80161.e: The rubber tree has a white, milky sap. Natural rubber is made from it.
80161.m: Natural rubber comes from the rubber tree.

80162.q: What is the jumping game with a long, stretched piece of elastic called?
80162.e: In French skipping, two children hold a long piece of elastic stretched around their legs. A third child jumps over it and into it.
80162.m: French skipping is a jumping game with elastic.

80163.q: What is a rubber band often used for in everyday life?
80163.e: A rubber band stretches around objects and squeezes them together. So it holds pencils or cards together, for example.
80163.m: A rubber band holds things together.

80164.q: What do you call a material that goes back to its old shape after being stretched?
80164.e: Elastic materials go back to their old shape after being pulled or pressed. Rubber is a good example.

80165.q: What does a typical metal spring look like?
80165.e: A coil spring is a wire that is wound like a spiral. This lets it squash together and stretch.
80165.m: A coil spring is a wound-up wire.

80166.q: What is built into many mattresses so that they give softly?
80166.e: A sprung mattress has lots of small springs inside. They give way under your body and push back again.

80167.q: What material are most springs made of?
80167.e: Springs are mostly made of steel wire. Steel is strong and springs back well.
80167.m: Most springs are made of steel.

80168.q: On many trampolines, what makes it possible to jump high?
a: Lots of springs around the edge
80168.e: Lots of springs are fixed around the edge of the trampoline. They stretch when you land and then fling you back up.

80169.q: Which writing tool often has a small spring inside?
80169.e: In a clicky ballpoint pen, a small spring pushes the refill back in when you click again.
80169.m: A ballpoint pen often has a small spring inside.

80170.q: Why do some bikes have springs?
80170.e: Suspension absorbs the bumps from stones and roots. So the ride is smoother, especially off-road.
80170.m: Springs on a bike absorb bumps.

80171.q: What squeezes a clothes peg shut?
80171.e: In the middle of a clothes peg there is a small metal spring. It presses the two halves together and holds the washing in place.
80171.m: A spring keeps a clothes peg closed.

80172.q: What do you tighten when you wind up a mechanical clock?
80172.e: A mechanical clock has a coiled spring inside. Winding tightens it, and it then drives the clock.
80172.m: A tightened spring drives a mechanical clock.

80173.q: What do we use to move our body?
80173.e: Muscles contract and so move the bones. Without muscles we could not move.

80174.q: Which force drives an ordinary bike without a motor?
80174.e: When you ride a bike, your legs push the pedals. The force for this comes from your muscles.
80174.m: A bike without a motor runs on muscle power.

80175.q: What are most muscles attached to?
a: The skin on the soles of the feet
80175.e: Muscles are attached to the bones by tendons. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on the bone and moves it.

80176.q: What can you feel in your muscles the day after doing a lot more sport than usual?
80176.e: After unusual effort, your muscles often ache. This is called muscle soreness, and it goes away after a few days.
80176.m: Sore muscles come after unusual effort.

80177.e: The biceps is a muscle at the front of the upper arm. It bends the arm, for example when you lift a bag.
80177.m: The biceps is on the upper arm.

80178.q: Which muscle works all your life without a break?
80178.e: The heart is a muscle. It pumps blood through the body day and night.
80178.m: The heart is a muscle that never takes a break.

80179.q: What is the largest muscle in the human body called?
80179.e: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body. It helps with walking, climbing stairs and standing up.
80179.m: The largest muscle is the gluteus maximus.

80180.q: Roughly how many muscles does a person have?
80180.e: A person has over 600 muscles. They work together when we move.

80181.q: What happens to a billiard ball that is lying still when another ball hits it?
a: It jumps up to the ceiling
80181.e: In the collision, the rolling ball passes on part of its momentum. The ball that was still starts to roll.
80181.m: A push can set a ball lying still in motion.

80182.q: Which way does a marble roll when you push it with your finger?
a: In the direction of the push
80182.e: A marble moves in the direction you push it. The direction of the force decides the direction of the movement.
80182.m: A marble rolls in the direction of the push.

80183.q: In which sport do you push a heavy metal ball as far as possible?
80183.e: In shot put, you push the ball powerfully forwards from your neck. Whoever puts it furthest wins.
80183.m: In shot put you push a ball a long way.

80184.q: In which Swiss tradition do you throw a heavy stone as far as possible?
80184.e: Stone putting (Steinstossen) is an old Swiss competition. The heavy Unspunnen stone is famous.
80184.m: Stone putting is a Swiss tradition.

80185.q: What knocks over the pins in skittles?
a: The push of the rolling ball
80185.e: The ball rolls against the pins and knocks into them. This makes the pins fall over.
80185.m: In skittles, the ball knocks over the pins.

80186.q: What protects your head from a hard knock when cycling?
80186.e: A cycle helmet has a thick layer of foam inside. In a fall, it absorbs the knock and protects the head.
80186.m: A cycle helmet protects your head from a knock.

80187.q: In a car, what absorbs the impact for the people in an accident?
80187.e: In an accident, the airbag inflates in a flash. It slows the body gently and absorbs the impact.
80187.m: The airbag absorbs the impact in an accident.

80188.q: What do you feel when another car bumps into yours on the dodgems?
80188.e: In the collision, a force acts on the car. You feel it as a strong jolt.
80188.m: In a collision you feel a jolt.

80189.q: What do you give a football when you kick it?
80189.e: When you kick, your foot touches the ball only very briefly. This short, strong push sends the ball flying.
80189.m: When you kick a ball, it gets a push.

80190.q: What is the throwing sport with a flat, round disc called?
80190.e: In the discus, you spin round and fling a flat, round disc of wood and metal a long way.
80190.m: In the discus you throw a round disc.

80191.q: What shape is the path of a ball that is thrown a long way?
80191.e: The ball first flies up and forwards and then falls down again. This makes an arc.
80191.m: A thrown ball flies in an arc.

80192.q: What helps you throw a ball further?
a: Throwing it with your eyes shut
80192.e: The more force you use when throwing, the faster the ball sets off. That is why it flies further.
80192.m: With more force, a ball flies further.

80193.q: Which object is thrown in athletics?
80193.e: In the javelin, you throw a long, pointed spear as far as possible.
80193.m: The javelin is thrown in athletics.

80194.q: What is special about a boomerang?
a: It can fly back to the thrower
80194.e: A boomerang has a special curved shape. Thrown correctly, it flies in an arc and comes back.

80195.q: In which game do you throw a ball into a high basket?
80195.e: In basketball, you throw the ball into a basket that hangs high up on a board. Every basket scores points.
80195.m: In basketball you throw the ball into the basket.

80196.q: In which game do you throw balls as close as possible to a small target ball?
80196.e: In boccia, you throw large balls. Whoever is closest to the small target ball gets points.
80196.m: In boccia you throw balls close to the target ball.

80197.q: Why do you swing your arm far back when throwing?
80197.e: When you swing far back, your arm can speed up the ball over a longer distance. So the ball gets more momentum.
80197.m: Swinging far back gives more momentum when throwing.

80198.q: What happens to modelling clay when you press it hard?
80198.e: Modelling clay changes shape when you press it and then stays in the new shape. That is why it is good for making figures.
80198.m: Modelling clay stays in the shape you press it into.

80199.q: What happens to a rubber ball when you squeeze it and let go again?
80199.e: The rubber ball only changes shape for a moment when squeezed. Afterwards it goes back to its round shape.
80199.m: A rubber ball becomes round again after being squeezed.

80200.q: What happens to an empty drinks can when you stand on it?
80200.e: The thin metal of the can cannot hold the weight. It bends and stays crushed.
80200.m: An empty can gets crushed under pressure.

80201.q: What happens to a glass bottle that falls onto a stone floor?
a: It bounces back like a ball
80201.e: Glass is hard but brittle. In a hard impact, it does not bend; it breaks.
80201.m: Glass breaks easily in a hard impact.

80202.q: What happens to loose snow when you squeeze it together firmly?
80202.e: When you squeeze, the snow is pressed together. It changes shape and becomes firm and hard.
80202.m: Snow becomes firm when squeezed together.

80203.q: Why can you see your footprints in wet sand?
a: Your foot presses the sand down
The wind blows the prints in
80203.e: The weight of your body presses the sand under your foot together. The sand keeps this shape as a print.
80203.m: Footprints form because your foot changes the shape of the sand.

80204.q: What happens to a thin branch when a bird sits on it?
80204.e: The bird's weight presses on the branch. That is why it bends down a little.
80204.m: A weight can bend a branch.

80205.q: What is it called when an object does not return to its old shape after being pressed?
80205.e: With permanent deformation, the object stays in its new shape. A dent in a bike mudguard is an example.
80205.m: A permanent deformation does not go away by itself.

80206.q: Where on a force meter do you read how big the force is?
80206.e: A force meter has a scale with numbers printed on it. A marker there shows how big the force is.
80206.m: You read the value on the scale.

80207.q: What is inside a simple force meter?
80207.e: A simple force meter contains a spring. The harder you pull, the further it stretches.
80207.m: There is a spring inside a force meter.

80208.q: What does a force meter show when you pull on it harder?
80208.e: When you pull harder, the spring stretches further. The pointer moves to a higher value.
80208.m: More force gives a higher value on the force meter.

80209.q: Roughly how many newtons does a force meter show when one kilogram hangs from it?
80209.e: On Earth, one kilogram pulls down with about 10 newtons. More exactly, it is about 9.8 newtons.
80209.m: One kilogram pulls down with about 10 newtons.

80210.q: What does a force meter show when nothing hangs from it and nobody is pulling?
80210.e: Without a force, the spring is not stretched. So the pointer is at zero.
80210.m: Without a force, the force meter shows zero.

80211.q: Which device works like a force meter and shows how heavy a suitcase is?
80211.e: A spring balance also has a spring inside. If you hang the suitcase from it, you can read how heavy it is.
80211.m: A spring balance works with a spring.

80212.q: What can happen if you put far too much load on a force meter?
a: The force meter starts to glow
80212.e: Every force meter has a maximum value. If you pull harder, the spring gets overstretched and no longer measures correctly.
80212.m: You should not overload a force meter.

a: A place where water comes out of the ground
A lake high up in the mountains
A place where a river ends
80310.e: At a spring, water comes out of the ground or out of a rock into the daylight. A stream often starts there.
80310.m: At a spring, water comes out of the earth.

80311.q: Why is spring water often cool even in summer?
a: It comes from the cool ground
It flows over blocks of ice
It falls from the sky at night
80311.e: Deep in the ground it stays about equally cool all year. That is why spring water is pleasantly fresh even on hot days.
80311.m: Spring water comes up cool from deep down.

80312.q: What is a spring called that warm water comes out of?
80312.e: The water of a thermal spring is heated deep inside the Earth. In Switzerland there are such springs in Baden or Leukerbad, for example.
80312.m: Warm water bubbles out of a thermal spring.

80313.q: What is a hot spring called that shoots water high into the air again and again?
80313.e: In a geyser, water underground gets so hot that it shoots upwards with steam. There are famous geysers in Iceland.
80313.m: A geyser shoots hot water into the air.

80314.q: Where does the water of the Rhône come from right at the start?
80314.e: The Rhône begins with meltwater from the Rhône Glacier in the canton of Valais.
80314.m: The Rhône begins at the Rhône Glacier in Valais.

80315.q: What is spring water with lots of dissolved minerals called that you can buy in bottles?
80315.e: On its way through the rock, water picks up minerals. Spring water like this is bottled and sold as mineral water.
80315.m: Mineral water comes from a spring.

80316.q: Can a spring dry up in summer?
a: Yes, if it does not rain for a long time
80316.e: A spring is fed by rain and snow that soak into the ground. If there is no rain for a long time, it can give less water or dry up completely.
80316.m: Without rain a spring can dry up.

80317.q: Where is the source of a river?
80317.e: A river begins at its source and then flows downhill. At the end it flows into another river, a lake or the sea.
80317.m: A river begins at its source.

a: A small body of flowing water
80318.e: A stream is smaller and narrower than a river. Its water keeps on flowing.
80318.m: A stream is a small body of flowing water.

80319.q: What forms when lots of streams flow together?
80319.e: Streams join together and get bigger and bigger. This is how a river forms.
80319.m: Lots of streams make a river.

80320.q: Which fish likes living in cool, clean streams?
80320.e: The brown trout needs cool water with lots of oxygen. It lives in many Swiss streams. Carp and catfish prefer warm, calm water.
80320.m: The trout likes cool, clean water.

80321.q: Which little creature under the stones in a stream shows that the water is clean?
80321.e: Freshwater shrimps need clean water with lots of oxygen. If you find lots of them, the stream is healthy.
80321.m: Lots of freshwater shrimps show the water is clean.

80322.q: Which bird dives in streams for small creatures?
80322.e: The dipper is a small songbird. It dives and even walks underwater along the bed of the stream.
80322.m: The dipper dives in streams for food.

80323.q: Which way does a stream flow?
80323.e: Because of gravity, water always flows downwards. That is why a stream flows downhill.

80324.q: Why does a mountain stream often flow very fast?
80324.e: The steeper the ground, the faster the water flows. In the mountains it is often very steep.
80324.m: The steeper the slope, the faster the stream.

80325.q: Which plant with yellow flowers likes to grow on wet stream banks in spring?
80325.e: The marsh marigold loves wet ground by streams and ditches. In spring its yellow flowers shine.
80325.m: The marsh marigold flowers yellow on stream banks.

80326.q: What does a beaver build in a stream?
80326.e: The beaver blocks the stream with branches and mud. This makes a pond where it can build its lodge safely.

a: Water that plunges over a rock step
Water that comes out of the ground
80327.e: In a waterfall, a stream or river flows over a steep step and falls down.
80327.m: A waterfall plunges down over a rock step.

80328.q: What can you often see in the fine spray of a waterfall when the sun is shining?
80328.e: The sun shines into the many tiny drops of water. These split the light into its colours.
80328.m: A rainbow often appears in the spray of a waterfall.

80329.q: What are the famous waterfalls between Canada and the USA called?
80329.e: Niagara Falls lie on the border between Canada and the USA. Millions of people visit them every year.
80329.m: Niagara Falls lie between Canada and the USA.

80330.q: What is the highest waterfall in the world called?
80330.e: Angel Falls is in Venezuela in South America. Its water falls almost 1000 metres.
80330.m: The highest waterfall in the world is Angel Falls.

80331.q: Which Swiss waterfalls plunge down inside a mountain?
80331.e: The Trümmelbach Falls thunder through a gorge inside the mountain near Lauterbrunnen. A lift takes visitors inside.
80331.m: The Trümmelbach Falls roar inside a mountain.

80332.q: What can the power of falling water be used for?
80332.e: Falling water drives turbines that make electricity. In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower.

80333.q: What is it called when people climb up frozen waterfalls in winter?
80333.e: In ice climbing, you climb up frozen waterfalls with ice axes and crampons. You only do this with training and safety ropes.
80333.m: You can go ice climbing on frozen waterfalls.

80334.q: Which village is the Staubbach Falls near?
80334.e: The Staubbach Falls plunge over a cliff into the valley right by the village of Lauterbrunnen.
80334.m: The Staubbach Falls are at Lauterbrunnen.

80335.q: Which canton are the Staubbach Falls in?
80335.e: The Staubbach Falls are in the Bernese Oberland, which is in the canton of Bern.
80335.m: The Staubbach Falls are in the canton of Bern.

80336.q: Roughly how high are the Staubbach Falls?
80336.e: The water of the Staubbach falls about 297 metres. It is one of the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.
80336.m: The Staubbach Falls are almost 300 metres high.

80337.q: Why are the Staubbach Falls called that? (“Staub” means dust in German.)
a: The water breaks up into fine droplets
They bring lots of dust into the valley
80337.e: On its long way down, the wind scatters the water in all directions. It then looks like fine dust.
80337.m: At the Staubbach Falls, the water turns into spray like dust.

80338.q: Which famous poet wrote a poem at the Staubbach Falls in 1779?
80338.e: Goethe visited the Staubbach Falls on a journey through Switzerland. There he wrote the poem “Song of the Spirits over the Waters”.
80338.m: Goethe wrote a poem at the Staubbach Falls.

80339.q: How can you get close to the Staubbach Falls in summer?
a: Through a gallery in the rock
By a lift in a tower
80339.e: In summer a path leads to a rock gallery at the Staubbach Falls. At other times the path is closed because of falling ice and rocks.
80339.m: In summer a path leads up to the Staubbach Falls.

80340.q: How does the water fall at the Staubbach Falls?
80340.e: The water plunges almost freely from the edge of the cliff. On the way down it turns into fine spray.
80340.m: The Staubbach falls freely over a cliff.

80341.q: When does the Staubbach carry the most water?
a: In early summer when the snow melts
80341.e: When the snow in the mountains melts in early summer, especially large amounts of water flow into the streams. In winter much of it is frozen.
80341.m: When the snow melts, mountain streams carry lots of water.

80342.q: Where does most of the drinking water in Switzerland come from?
80342.e: About 80 per cent of Swiss drinking water comes from groundwater and springs. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
80342.m: Most of Switzerland's drinking water comes from groundwater.

80343.q: What is used today to bring groundwater up from deep down?
80343.e: Pumps suck the groundwater up through pipes. Then it flows into the water mains.

80344.q: Why is groundwater often very clean?
80344.e: On its way through soil, sand and gravel, lots of bits of dirt get caught. The ground works like a filter.

a: Poison or too much fertiliser in the soil
80345.e: Whatever soaks into the ground can reach the groundwater. That is why you must never pour poison or oil onto the ground.
80345.m: Poison in the soil can pollute groundwater.

80346.q: How did people long ago get water up from a deep well?
a: With a bucket on a rope
80346.e: A well like this reaches down to the groundwater. People lowered a bucket on a rope and pulled it back up full of water.
80346.m: People used to get well water up with a bucket.

80347.q: Where in the ground is groundwater usually found?
a: In gaps between gravel and sand
In big caves full of air
80347.e: Groundwater fills the tiny spaces between small stones, gravel and sand. There is usually no open underground lake.
80347.m: Groundwater is in the gaps between gravel and sand.

a: Yes, as fast as a river
80348.e: Groundwater moves slowly through the ground, often only a few metres a day. It flows towards rivers or lakes.

80349.q: What happens to groundwater if it does not rain for a very long time?
a: It gets as warm as a bath
80349.e: Without rain, no new water comes in. The water table then slowly drops.
80349.m: In a drought, the groundwater sinks.

a: When the ground is completely dry
80350.e: Rainwater flows into small dips in the ground. If it cannot soak away quickly, a puddle is left.
80350.m: Puddles collect in dips after rain.

80351.q: Why do puddles on tarmac stay for a long time?
a: Tarmac does not let water through
80351.e: Tarmac is sealed, so the water cannot soak into the ground. It stays there until it evaporates or drains away.
80351.m: Tarmac does not let rainwater through.

80352.q: Where does a puddle go on a sunny day?
a: A bird drinks it all up
80352.e: The warmth of the sun makes the water evaporate. It becomes invisible water vapour in the air.

80353.q: What shimmers in a puddle when a little oil is floating on it?
80353.e: A very thin layer of oil on the water makes the light shimmer in bright colours.
80353.m: Oil on a puddle shimmers in many colours.

80354.q: What happens to a puddle on a frosty night?
80354.e: Below 0 degrees, water turns into ice. In the morning the puddle is then often covered with a layer of ice.
80354.m: Puddles freeze when there is frost.

80355.q: Which birds collect wet mud from puddles to build their nests?
80355.e: Swallows make little balls out of damp mud. They use them to stick their nests under a roof, for example.
80355.m: Swallows build their nests from mud.

80356.q: What do you see when you look into a still puddle?
80356.e: The smooth surface of the water reflects the light like a mirror. That is why you see yourself and the sky.
80356.m: A still puddle reflects like a mirror.

80357.q: Which insects like to lay their eggs in puddles and water butts?
80357.e: Mosquitoes need still water for their larvae. Even a small puddle can be enough.
80357.m: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water.

80358.q: Which animals sometimes lay their eggs in puddles in wheel ruts?
80358.e: Some toads, such as the yellow-bellied toad, like small, warm puddles, for example in wheel ruts. They lay their spawn there.
80358.m: Toads also lay their eggs in puddles.

80359.q: On which nights does a lot of dew form?
80359.e: Without clouds, the ground cools down a lot at night. Without wind, the water from the air can then settle easily on the grass.
80359.m: Clear, calm nights bring lots of dew.

80360.q: Where does the water in dewdrops come from?
a: From water vapour in the air
80360.e: There is invisible water vapour in the air. When the air cools down, it turns back into liquid water in small drops.
80360.m: Dew forms from water vapour in the air.

80361.q: What happens to dew when the sun shines in the morning?
a: It turns into fog in the ground
80361.e: The sun warms the grass and the air. The drops then turn back into water vapour.

80362.q: Where do dewdrops glitter especially beautifully in the morning?
80362.e: Lots of little drops hang on the fine threads of a spider's web. In the morning light they glitter like pearls.
80362.m: Dewdrops glitter like pearls on spiders' webs.

80363.q: What happens to cold glasses when you come into a warm room?
a: They steam up with tiny droplets
80363.e: The warm air in the room contains water vapour. On the cold glasses it turns into tiny drops, just like dew.
80363.m: Water droplets form on cold surfaces.

80364.q: On a clear night, when is it usually coolest?
80364.e: The ground cools down all night long. That is why it is usually coldest at sunrise, and there is lots of dew.
80364.m: It is often coolest at sunrise.

80365.q: Why is there often less dew under a tree in the morning?
a: The ground there cools down less
The sun shines there at night
80365.e: The treetop works like a blanket and holds back some warmth. The ground underneath gets less cold, so less dew forms.
80365.m: Under trees it cools down less and there is less dew.

a: Fine ice crystals on branches and grass
80366.e: Hoar frost is made of lots of tiny ice crystals. They grow on trees, fences and grass.
80366.m: Hoar frost is made of fine ice crystals.

80367.q: In what weather does hoar frost form?
a: When it is frosty and the air is damp
When it is hot and sunny
80367.e: Hoar frost forms when it is colder than 0 degrees and the air is damp, for example in fog. The tiny droplets freeze onto everything they touch.
80367.m: Hoar frost needs frost and damp air.

80368.e: The many fine ice crystals scatter the light. That is why hoar frost looks white.

80369.q: In which season do we see hoar frost in Switzerland?
80369.e: Hoar frost needs temperatures below 0 degrees. In Switzerland that happens mainly in winter and on cold autumn nights.
80369.m: You see hoar frost mainly in winter.

80370.q: On which side of the twigs does hoar frost grow most?
a: On the side the wind comes from
On the side facing the ground
80370.e: The wind carries the damp, cold air against the twigs. Where it hits them, the ice crystals grow the most.
80370.m: Hoar frost grows towards the wind.

80371.q: What are the patterns of ice called that grow on cold window panes?
80371.e: On cold panes the moisture freezes into branching patterns. They look like flowers made of ice.
80371.m: Frost flowers are ice patterns on windows.

80372.q: What can happen when a lot of hoar frost hangs on trees?
80372.e: Thick hoar frost can get very heavy. Then the branches bend and some break off.
80372.m: Heavy hoar frost can break branches.

80373.q: What happens to hoar frost when it gets warmer?
80373.e: When the temperature rises above 0 degrees, the ice crystals melt. They often fall off the branches like fine snow, too.
80373.m: Hoar frost melts when it gets warmer.

a: Dripping water freezes bit by bit
80374.e: Water runs down an edge and freezes drop by drop. This makes the icicle longer and longer.

80375.q: Why is it dangerous to walk under big icicles?
80375.e: Big icicles are heavy and pointed. If they come loose, they can hurt people.
80375.m: It is better not to walk under big icicles.

80376.q: In what weather do icicles grow especially well?
a: The sun melts snow, but the air is cold
80376.e: The sun melts some snow on the roof. The water drips down and freezes into ice in the cold air.
80376.m: Icicles grow when melting snow freezes in cold air.

80377.q: Which way do icicles grow on a roof?
80377.e: Because of gravity, the water drips downwards. That is why icicles grow from the top down.

80378.q: What happens to icicles when it thaws?
a: They get as hard as stone
80378.e: When it gets warmer than 0 degrees, the ice melts. The icicles drip and get smaller until they fall off.

80379.q: Why are icicles pointed at the bottom?
a: The least water reaches the bottom
Birds peck them into a point
80379.e: Most of the water freezes further up the icicle. Only a little reaches the tip, so it stays thin.
80379.m: Icicles are thick at the top and pointed at the bottom.

80380.q: Where in nature can very long icicles hang in winter?
80380.e: In winter, water seeps out of cracks in the rocks. It freezes and sometimes forms icicles several metres long.
80380.m: Huge icicles grow on rock faces in winter.

a: A very wet area with soft ground
80381.e: In a bog the ground is full of water and very soft. You can sink into it.
80381.m: A bog is a wet area with soft ground.

80382.q: Which animals like living in a wet bog?
80382.e: In a bog there is lots of water and lots of insects. That is why frogs feel at home there.

80383.q: Why are many bogs in Switzerland protected?
a: Rare plants and animals live there
Lots of vegetables are grown there
The best ski slopes are there
Most of the timber grows there
80383.e: In bogs there are plants and animals that are hardly found anywhere else. That is why many bogs are protected.
80383.m: Bogs are home to rare plants and animals.

80384.q: Which small meat-eating plant grows in Swiss bogs?
80384.e: The sundew has sticky drops on its leaves. Small insects get stuck to them and are digested.
80384.m: The sundew catches insects with sticky drops.

80385.q: Who decided in 1987 that bogs in Switzerland should be specially protected?
80385.e: In the vote on the Rothenthurm initiative, the people said yes to protecting bogs. Since then this has been in the Federal Constitution.
80385.m: The Swiss people decided to protect bogs in 1987.

80386.q: Why can a bog store so much water?
a: The moss soaks up water like a sponge
The ground is made of hard rock
Lots of big trees grow there
80386.e: Peat moss can hold many times its own weight in water. This is how the bog holds on to lots of water.
80386.m: A bog stores water like a sponge.

80387.q: Why should you stay on the paths in a bog?
a: You can sink in and trample plants
It is warmer on the paths
It is too dark beside the paths
80387.e: The soft ground of the bog cannot hold you everywhere. Also, rare plants grow there that are easily damaged.
80387.m: In a bog, you stay on the paths.

80388.q: What colour is the water in a raised bog often?
80388.e: Substances from dead plants dissolve in the water. They turn it brown like tea.
80388.m: Bog water is often brown like tea.

a: A small, shallow body of still water
80389.e: A pond is small and so shallow that plants often grow right down to the bottom. The water hardly flows.
80389.m: A pond is a small, shallow body of water.

80390.q: Which animals lay their spawn in the pond in spring?
80390.e: Frogs lay their eggs in the water as spawn. The clumps of eggs float in the pond.
80390.m: Frogs lay spawn in the pond in spring.

80391.q: What are young frogs called that still live in the water?
80391.e: Tadpoles hatch from frogspawn. They have a tail and breathe with gills until they become frogs.

80392.q: Which insect with shimmering wings hunts mosquitoes over ponds?
80392.e: Dragonflies are fast fliers and catch other insects in the air. Their larvae live in the water.
80392.m: Dragonflies hunt mosquitoes over the water.

80393.q: Which insect can walk on the surface of the water?
80393.e: The pond skater is very light and has long legs with fine hairs. That is why it does not sink.
80393.m: The pond skater walks on water.

80394.q: Which plant with big round leaves floats on ponds?
80394.e: The water lily has its roots in the mud at the bottom. Its leaves and flowers float on the water.
80394.m: The water lily floats on the pond.

80395.q: Which plant on the edge of a pond has brown heads that look like sausages?
80395.e: The bulrush grows in shallow water at the edge. Its brown heads are full of seeds.
80395.m: The bulrush has brown heads at the water's edge.

80396.q: Why does a pond freeze over faster in winter than a big lake?
a: It is always in a forest
80396.e: A small, shallow pond holds little water. It cools down quickly and therefore freezes over sooner than a big, deep lake.
80396.m: Small, shallow ponds freeze over quickly.

80397.q: Which bird often swims on ponds, with the male having a shiny green head?
80397.e: The mallard is the most common duck in Switzerland. You can recognise the male by its shimmering green head.
80397.m: The male mallard has a green head.

80398.q: Why can you not drink seawater?
80398.e: Seawater contains a lot of salt. If you drink it, you get even thirstier, because your body has to get rid of the salt.
80398.m: Seawater is too salty to drink.

80399.q: Is there more sea or more land on Earth?
80399.e: Most of the Earth is covered by sea. That is why the Earth is also called the blue planet.
80399.m: Most of the Earth is covered by sea.

80400.q: Which sea does the Rhine flow into in the end?
80400.e: The Rhine flows from Switzerland through Germany and the Netherlands. There it flows into the North Sea.
80400.m: The Rhine flows into the North Sea.

80401.q: Which sea does the Rhône flow into in the end?
80401.e: The Rhône flows through Lake Geneva and then through France. It flows into the Mediterranean in southern France.
80401.m: The Rhône flows into the Mediterranean.

80402.q: Which sea does the water of the Inn from the Engadine reach?
80402.e: The Inn flows into the Danube. The Danube finally flows into the Black Sea.
80402.m: The water of the Inn reaches the Black Sea.

80403.q: What is the largest animal in the sea?
80403.e: The blue whale can grow over 30 metres long. It is even the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth.
80403.m: The blue whale is the largest animal in the world.

80405.q: What do you do with finely chopped red cabbage to get red cabbage juice?
80405.e: The hot water draws the colour out of the leaves. After cooling, you pour the coloured juice through a sieve.
80405.m: Hot water draws the colour out of red cabbage.

80406.q: What colour is red cabbage juice in pure water?
80406.e: In water that is neither acidic nor basic, red cabbage juice is purple. Only when you add something does the colour change.
80406.m: In pure water, red cabbage juice is purple.

80407.q: What colour does red cabbage juice turn when you stir in bicarbonate of soda?
80407.e: Bicarbonate of soda is not acidic but basic. That is why the purple red cabbage juice turns blue to blue-green.
80407.m: Bicarbonate of soda turns red cabbage juice blue.

80408.q: What does red cabbage juice show with its colour?
80408.e: The dye in red cabbage changes colour depending on whether a substance is acidic or basic. This lets you test things from the kitchen.
80408.m: Red cabbage juice shows by its colour whether something is acidic.

80409.q: What do you call a substance that shows by its colour whether something is acidic?
80409.e: An indicator is something that shows. Red cabbage juice is an indicator you can make yourself.
80409.m: An indicator shows by its colour whether something is acidic.

80410.q: What does a splash of vinegar do to the colour when cooking red cabbage?
80410.e: Acid from vinegar or sour apples keeps red cabbage red. Without acid it tends to turn bluish when cooked.
80410.m: With a little acid, cooked red cabbage stays red.

80411.q: What property does lemon juice have if it turns red cabbage juice red?
80411.e: Lemon juice contains acid. Acidic substances turn red cabbage juice red.
80411.m: Acidic substances turn red cabbage juice red.

80412.q: Which juice, like red cabbage juice, changes colour with acid?
80412.e: Blueberries contain a blue dye similar to red cabbage. That is why their juice also changes colour with acid.
80412.m: Blueberry juice also changes colour with acid.

80413.q: What is food colouring used for?
80413.e: Food colouring is safe to eat. It is used, for example, to colour cakes, icing or Easter eggs.

80414.q: Which colour do you get when you mix red and yellow food colouring?
80414.e: Red and yellow together make orange. This way you can mix many new colours from just a few.
80414.m: Red and yellow together make orange.

80415.q: Which vegetable colours food bright red?
80415.e: Beetroot contains a strong red dye. Hands and clothes quickly turn red from it too.

80416.e: Turmeric is a yellow powder made from a root. It colours curries yellow, for example.

80417.q: In which water does a drop of food colouring spread faster?
80417.e: In warm water the tiniest particles move faster. That is why the colour spreads more quickly there.
80417.m: Colour spreads faster in warm water than in cold.

80418.q: What happens to a white flower that stands in water with food colouring for a few days?
a: The flower loses all its leaves
The flower grows twice as big
80418.e: The flower sucks the coloured water up through its stem. This way the colour reaches the flower head.
80418.m: A flower sucks water up through its stem to the flower head.

80419.q: Which vegetable provides a green colouring for food?
80419.e: Spinach contains a lot of green leaf pigment. You can use spinach to colour pasta green, for example.

80420.q: Which letter do the numbers of colourings on packaging start with?
80420.e: Additives such as colourings have an E number on packaging. Colourings have the numbers E 100 to E 199.
80420.m: Colourings are listed on packaging with an E number.

80421.q: You want to separate the colours of a felt-tip pen with water. Which paper do you put the dot of colour on?
80421.e: Coffee filter paper soaks up water well. The water can travel upwards in it and carry the colours with it.
80421.m: To separate colours, you need paper that soaks up water well.

80422.q: A coffee filter with a felt-tip dot stands in water. What travels up the paper and takes the colour with it?
80422.e: The paper soaks water up from the glass. The water dissolves the colour and carries it along.
80422.m: The water carries the colours up the paper.

80423.q: You draw a dot with a black felt-tip pen on a coffee filter and stand it in water. What do you soon see?
a: No colour at all any more
80423.e: Black felt-tip ink is often mixed from several colours. On the paper they separate, for example into blue, yellow and red.
80423.m: Black ink is often mixed from several colours.

80424.q: Where must the dot of colour be on the paper strip when it goes into the water?
80424.e: If the dot is in the water, the colour simply dissolves in the glass. If it is just above, the water rises up to it.
80424.m: The dot of colour must be just above the water.

80425.q: Which pens can you use to separate colours in paper with water?
80425.e: The colour must dissolve in water, otherwise it just stays put. That is why washable felt-tip pens work best.
80425.m: To separate colours with water, you need washable felt-tip pens.

80426.q: What does the Greek word ‘chroma’ in chromatography mean?
80426.e: ‘Chroma’ is the Greek word for colour. So chromatography means roughly ‘colour writing’.

80427.q: A coffee filter with a felt-tip dot stands in water. Why do different stripes of colour appear?
80427.e: Some colours are easily carried along by the water, others tend to stay behind. So they get different distances and separate.
80427.m: Each colour travels a different distance in the paper.

80428.q: Which pigments can you separate from green leaves with chromatography?
80428.e: Green leaves contain not only green but also yellow pigment. With methylated spirits instead of water, and with the help of an adult, you can separate them.
80428.m: Green leaves also contain yellow pigment.

80429.q: What can you use to make a simple invisible ink?
