80796.e: You stamp with your foot. That is why the foot symbol stands for stamping.
80796.m: Symbols in instructions show which part of the body moves.

80797.q: What do you need so that everyone in the group dances at the same time?
80797.e: If everyone listens to the same beat, they do the steps at the same time.
80797.m: A shared beat keeps a dance group together.

80798.q: Dance: right, left, right, left and so on. Which is the 5th step?
80798.e: Odd-numbered steps are right, even-numbered steps are left. The 5th step is therefore right.
80798.m: A pattern helps you predict the next step.

80799.q: Dance instructions have 4 steps. You dance them 3 times in a row. How many steps is that?

80800.q: In musical statues, the music suddenly stops. What must everyone do?
80800.e: In musical statues the rule is: music off means stand still. Anyone who moves is out.
80800.m: In musical statues you stand still when the music stops.

80801.q: What colour is a ripe acorn usually?
80801.e: Young acorns are green. When they are ripe in autumn, they turn brown and shiny.

80802.q: Why don’t we humans eat raw acorns?
80802.e: Acorns contain lots of tannins. These taste very bitter and are bad for your tummy when raw.
80802.m: Raw acorns are not for us humans.

80803.q: Which farm animals did people once drive into the woods in autumn to eat acorns?
80803.e: In the past farmers fed their pigs in oak woods in autumn. This was called pannage.
80803.m: Pigs used to eat acorns in the woods.

80804.q: On which playing cards is the acorn one of the four suits?
80804.e: German Swiss Jass cards have the suits acorns, bells, roses and shields. The French cards have hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades.
80804.m: In Jass there is a suit called acorns.

80805.q: What does the husk that beechnuts grow in look like?
80805.e: Beechnuts grow in a woody husk with soft spines. When it is ripe, it splits open into four flaps.
80805.m: The beechnut husk splits open in autumn.

80806.q: How many beechnuts are usually in one husk?
80806.e: Usually two beechnuts lie together in one husk.
80806.m: A beech husk usually holds two beechnuts.

80807.q: Why shouldn’t you eat lots of raw beechnuts?
80807.e: Raw beechnuts contain substances that can cause tummy ache and sickness in larger amounts. Roasted, they are easier to digest.
80807.m: Beechnuts are best eaten roasted, and only a few.

80808.q: What did people once press out of beechnuts?
80808.e: Beechnuts contain a lot of fat. Especially in hard times, people pressed oil for cooking from them.
80808.m: You can press oil from beechnuts.

80809.q: What do you call a year in which beeches bear especially many fruits?
80809.e: Beeches do not bear the same amount of fruit every year. In a mast year, especially many beechnuts hang on the trees.
80809.m: In a mast year there are especially many beechnuts.

80810.q: Which birds come to Switzerland in their millions in some winters to eat beechnuts?
80810.e: In years with lots of beechnuts, bramblings come to us from the north in huge flocks. They spend the night together at big roosts.

80811.q: What are roasted sweet chestnuts called in Switzerland?
80811.e: Hot Marroni are roasted sweet chestnuts. In winter you can buy them in town at a chestnut stall.

80812.q: What does the case of the sweet chestnut look like?
a: Green with lots of sharp spines
80812.e: The sweet chestnut grows in a case with very many sharp spines. It is best to touch it with gloves.
80812.m: The sweet chestnut case prickles like a hedgehog.

80813.q: In which canton are there especially many sweet chestnut trees?
80813.e: In Ticino sweet chestnuts grow in large forests on the sunny slopes.

80814.q: Which Swiss dessert is made from chestnut purée?
80814.e: For vermicelles, sweet chestnut purée is pressed through a press. It then looks like thin noodles.
80814.m: Vermicelles look like noodles but are made of chestnuts.

80815.q: What was the chestnut tree once called in the southern valleys of Switzerland?
80815.e: People in the south of Switzerland used to eat chestnuts almost every day. They filled you up like bread, which is why the tree was called the bread tree.
80815.m: The chestnut was once a staple food in Ticino.

80816.e: The chestnuts ripen in October. Then the spiky cases fall from the tree and burst open.

80817.q: What is a well-tended chestnut grove in Ticino called?
80817.e: A Selve is a chestnut grove that is looked after like a garden. Grass grows under the trees so that you can pick up the chestnuts easily.
80817.m: In Ticino a chestnut grove is called a Selve.

80818.q: Why do you cut a slit in chestnuts before roasting them?
80818.e: When the chestnut is heated, steam forms inside it. The cut lets the steam escape; otherwise the shell can burst with a bang.
80818.m: You cut chestnuts so that they don’t burst.

80819.q: How many chestnuts are usually in one spiky case?
80819.e: A sweet chestnut case usually holds one to three fruits.
80819.m: A chestnut case holds only a few fruits.

80820.q: What lies between the scales of a fir cone?
80820.e: The tree’s seeds lie between the scales. The cone protects them until they are ripe.
80820.m: A cone is the seed house of a conifer.

80821.q: What does a fir cone do when it rains?
80821.e: When it is wet, the scales close so that the seeds stay dry. In dry weather they open again.
80821.m: A cone is a little weather forecaster.

80822.q: Which animal gnaws fir cones until only the core is left?
80822.e: The squirrel bites off the scales to get at the seeds. What is left is a gnawed core with a few scales at the tip.
80822.m: Gnawed cones give the squirrel away.

80823.q: Which bird wedges fir cones into a crack to peck out the seeds?
80823.e: The great spotted woodpecker wedges the cone into a crack in the wood. This workplace is called a woodpecker’s anvil.
80823.m: At its anvil the woodpecker pecks cones open.

80824.q: What often sticks to fresh fir cones?
80824.e: Conifers make sticky resin. It protects the tree and often sticks to cones and hands.
80824.m: Resin is the sticky sap of conifers.

80825.q: Why do the seeds in a fir cone have a little wing?
a: So that the wind can carry them away
So that birds can see them better
80825.e: When the seeds fall out of the cone, they glide through the air on their wing. So they land further away from the parent tree.
80825.m: Winged seeds travel on the wind.

80826.q: How many wings does a maple fruit have while it is still whole?
80826.e: Maple fruits grow as a pair with two wings. Later they split into two parts, each with one seed.
80826.m: A whole maple fruit has two wings.

80827.q: What colour are maple seeds when they are ripe in autumn?
80827.e: When maple seeds are ripe and dry in autumn, they turn brown.
80827.m: Ripe maple seeds are brown and dry.

80828.q: Where is the actual seed in a maple fruit?
a: In the thick part at the end of the wing
Right at the tip of the wing
80828.e: The seed is in the round, thick part. The thin wing attached to it is only there for flying.
80828.m: In a maple fruit the seed is in the thick lump.

80829.q: What do you call fruits with a flat wing, like those of the maple?
80829.e: Fruits with a wing are called winged fruits. The ash and the elm have fruits like this too.

80830.q: What is the best way to open a hazelnut?
80830.e: The shell of the hazelnut is very hard. You can crack it open with a nutcracker.
80830.m: The hazelnut has a hard shell.

80834.q: Which sweet is made from roasted hazelnuts?
80834.e: For nougat, roasted hazelnuts are ground finely and mixed with sugar, often with chocolate too.

80835.q: Which country harvests the most hazelnuts in the world?
80835.e: Turkey harvests far more than half of all the world’s hazelnuts. They grow there on the Black Sea coast.

80836.q: What does the husk around a young hazelnut look like?
80836.e: Young hazelnuts sit in a green husk that looks like ragged leaves.
80836.m: The young hazelnut sits in a green leafy husk.

80837.q: Which plant do rose hips come from?
80837.e: Rose hips are the fruits of roses. After flowering, a fruit grows in late summer.
80837.m: A rose flower turns into a rose hip.

80838.q: What colour are ripe rose hips usually?
80838.e: Ripe rose hips are bright red or orange-red. They are only green while they are unripe.
80838.m: Ripe rose hips are bright red.

80839.q: What did children once make from the seeds of rose hips?
80839.e: The seeds of rose hips are covered in fine little hairs. These scratch the skin, so they were used as itching powder.
80839.m: The little hairs in rose hips make your skin itch.

80840.q: Which vitamin is found in especially large amounts in rose hips?
80840.e: Rose hips contain lots of vitamin C, even more than lemons.
80840.m: Rose hips are little vitamin C bombs.

80841.q: Which drink is often made from dried rose hips?
80841.e: You pour hot water over dried rose hips. This makes a reddish tea.
80841.m: Rose hip tea has a lovely red colour.

80842.q: Which wild rose produces lots of rose hips in hedges?
80842.e: The dog rose is the most common wild rose in Switzerland. It has pink flowers and lots of rose hips in autumn.
80842.m: The dog rose is a wild rose.

80843.q: What is often made from rose hips in the kitchen?
80843.e: Rose hips make a delicious jam. The seeds are removed first.
80843.m: Rose hip jam is a tasty spread.

80844.q: Who likes eating rose hips that are still on the bush in winter?
80844.e: Many rose hips stay on the bush into winter. Blackbirds and other birds find food in them when there is little else.
80844.m: Rose hips are winter food for birds.

80845.q: Rowan berries grow on the rowan tree. What is another name for this tree?
80845.e: The rowan is also called the mountain ash. But it is not related to the ash.
80845.m: The rowan, or mountain ash, has rowan berries.

80846.q: What colour are ripe rowan berries?
80846.e: In late summer and autumn the berries turn bright orange-red.

80847.q: In German, rowan berries are called “bird berries”. Why?
80847.e: Blackbirds, thrushes and many other birds love eating the berries. They spread the seeds in their droppings.
80847.m: Rowan berries are a feast for birds.

80848.q: What do raw rowan berries taste like?
80848.e: Raw rowan berries are bitter. If you eat a lot of them, you can get tummy ache.

80849.q: What happens to rowan berries when you cook them?
80849.e: Cooking breaks down the substance that causes tummy ache. That is why you can make jam from rowan berries.
80849.m: You can eat cooked rowan berries.

80850.q: What do the leaves of the rowan look like?
a: Like a hand with five fingers
80850.e: A rowan leaf is made of many small leaflets. This is called pinnate, or feathery.

80851.q: Where does the rowan grow in Switzerland?
a: From the lowlands high up into the mountains
80851.e: The rowan is very tough. It even grows high up in the mountains, where other broadleaved trees are missing.
80851.m: The rowan is a tough tree.

80852.q: How do rowan berries hang on the tree?
a: One by one on long threads
80852.e: Lots of rowan berries hang together in big, heavy bunches. That is why you can see them from far away.
80852.m: Rowan berries grow in thick bunches.

80853.q: About how big are the fruits of the lime tree?
a: About as big as a pea
As big as a hen’s egg
80853.e: Lime fruits are very small. They are only about as big as a pea.

80854.e: The fruits of the lime tree are small balls. Several often hang together on thin stalks.

80855.q: What is made from the dried flowers of the lime tree?
80855.e: Dried lime flowers make a popular tea. Many people like drinking it when they have a cold.
80855.m: People like drinking lime blossom tea when they have a cold.

80856.e: Birch seeds are tiny and weigh almost nothing. Even a light breath of wind can carry them away.
80856.m: Birch seeds are as light as a feather.

80857.q: What does a birch seed have on its left and right?
80857.e: The seed sits in the middle and has two tiny see-through wings. So it looks like a tiny insect.
80857.m: Birch seeds have two little wings.

80858.q: Which small bird, whose German name contains the word birch, likes eating birch seeds?
80858.e: The redpoll is a small finch with a little red cap. It pecks the seeds out of birch catkins.

80859.q: Where do birch seeds sometimes even sprout?
a: In gutters and cracks in walls
In the middle of the sea
80859.e: Because the wind carries the seeds everywhere, young birches even sprout in gutters and cracks in walls.
80859.m: Birches grow almost anywhere a seed lands.

80860.q: What do young birches especially need to grow?
80860.e: Young birches only grow well when lots of sun falls on them. In a dark forest they hardly stand a chance.

80861.q: How do larch cones sit on the twig?
80861.e: The small larch cones sit upright on the twigs, like little candles.
80861.m: Larch cones sit upright on the twig.

80862.q: What do many larch cones do after the seeds have fallen out?
a: They stay on the twig for years
80862.e: Empty larch cones often stay on the tree for several years. That is why in winter you see lots of small cones on bare larches.
80862.m: Larch cones stay on the tree for a long time.

80863.q: What colour are very young larch cones in spring?
80863.e: In spring the young female flowers that turn into cones glow pink to dark red. They look like little roses.
80863.m: Young larch cones look like little roses.

80864.q: How do the seeds of the Swiss stone pine get to a new place?
a: They jump out of the cone
80864.e: Swiss stone pine nuts are heavy and cannot fly. Animals like the spotted nutcracker carry them away and hide them in the ground.
80864.m: Animals carry Swiss stone pine nuts to new places.

80865.q: How does a ripe Swiss stone pine cone open?
a: It doesn’t; animals break it open
It bursts open with a bang
80865.e: Swiss stone pine cones stay closed. Animals peck or gnaw them open, or they slowly break apart on the ground.
80865.m: Swiss stone pine cones do not open by themselves.

80866.q: How long does a Swiss stone pine cone take to ripen?
80866.e: From flower to ripeness takes about two years for the Swiss stone pine. The cones only ripen in the autumn after the year they flowered.
80866.m: Swiss stone pine cones take two years to ripen.

80867.q: About how old is an oak when it bears acorns for the first time?
80867.e: Oaks grow slowly. A young oak only bears its first acorns after many years, often after 40 years or more.
80867.m: Oaks need a lot of patience before they bear acorns.

80868.q: What grows from an acorn that sprouts in the ground?
80868.e: The acorn contains the tree’s seed. In spring a little seedling can grow from it.
80868.m: A small acorn can become a huge tree.

80869.q: In botany, what is an acorn?
80869.e: The acorn has a hard shell and a seed inside. That is why it counts as a nut.

80870.q: What did people make from roasted acorns in hard times?
80870.e: When there was no real coffee, people roasted acorns and made a coffee-like drink from them.
80870.m: People once made coffee substitute from acorns.

80871.q: What does an acorn sit in on the twig?
80871.e: The bottom of the acorn sits in a little cup, like an egg in an egg cup. When it falls off, the cup often stays on the twig.
80871.m: The acorn sits in a little cup.

80872.q: Which animal likes collecting beechnuts as a store in autumn?
80872.e: Squirrels collect beechnuts and nuts in autumn. They hide them as a store for the winter.

80873.q: What colour is the shell of a ripe beechnut?
80873.e: Ripe beechnuts have a smooth, shiny brown shell. Inside is a pale kernel.

80875.q: What is the name of a chestnut festival in Ticino?
80875.e: At a Castagnata in autumn, chestnuts are roasted over a fire and eaten together.
80875.m: In Ticino people celebrate the chestnut with a Castagnata.

80876.e: Spruce, fir, pine, larch and Swiss stone pine have cones. Broadleaved trees have other fruits.
80876.m: Cones are the fruits of conifers.

80877.q: What do you fill a fir cone with to make bird food?
80877.e: You press a mixture of fat and seeds between the scales. Then you hang the cone on a string in a tree.
80877.m: A filled cone makes tasty bird food.

80878.q: Why is it good for a young maple if its seed flies far away?
a: It has more light and space there
80878.e: Under the big parent tree it is shady and crowded. Further away, the little maple has more light and space to grow.
80878.m: Young trees need light and space.

80879.q: When do maple seeds usually sprout?
80879.e: The seeds lie on the ground through the winter. In spring, when it gets warmer, they sprout.

80880.q: What colour are unripe maple seeds in summer?
80880.e: In summer maple fruits are still green and soft. Sometimes they have a reddish tinge too.

80881.q: How does a maple seed fall from the tree?
a: It drops straight like a stone
80881.e: The wing makes the maple seed spin. So it falls slowly and the wind can carry it far.
80881.m: Maple seeds spin like little propellers.

80882.q: How can you tell that a mouse has eaten a hazelnut?
a: By a round hole in the shell
By a knot in the stalk
80882.e: Mice gnaw a round hole in the shell. Squirrels, on the other hand, usually split the nut into two halves.
80882.m: Gnaw marks on nuts show who ate them.

80883.q: Why do squirrels collect hazelnuts in autumn?
a: As a store for the winter
To give them to their young
80883.e: In autumn squirrels bury nuts in lots of places. In winter they look for these stores again.
80883.m: Squirrels store nuts for the winter.

80884.q: When are rose hips especially soft and sweet?
80884.e: After the first frost, rose hips get softer and taste milder. That is why people like to collect them late in autumn.
80884.m: Frost makes rose hips soft and mild.

80885.q: What does the flesh of a ripe rose hip taste like?
80885.e: The flesh of the rose hip tastes fruity, sweet and a little sour.
80885.m: Rose hips taste sweet and sour.

80886.q: Where do rose hips often grow in nature?
a: In hedges and at the edge of woods
In the middle of a lake
80886.e: Wild roses like to grow in hedges, at woodland edges and along paths. There you find lots of rose hips in autumn.
80886.m: You can find rose hips in hedges.

80887.q: What colour are the flowers of the rowan in spring?
80887.e: In May and June the rowan has large white clusters of flowers. Later the berries grow from them.

80888.q: What did bird catchers once use rowan berries for?
80888.e: In the past people caught birds with traps in which they put rowan berries. The berries attracted the birds.
80888.m: Rowan berries once lured birds into traps.

80889.e: The lime fruit has a firm shell with a seed inside. That is why it is called a small nut.
80889.m: The lime tree has small nuts.

80890.q: How long do many lime fruits stay hanging on the tree?
80890.e: Many lime fruits still hang on the bare branches long after the leaves have fallen. Then the winter wind carries them away.
80890.m: Lime fruits often stay on the tree into winter.

80891.q: What does the shell of a lime fruit feel like?
80891.e: The small lime fruits are covered in fine little hairs. That is why they feel slightly fuzzy.

80892.q: About how many seeds does a big birch produce in one year?
80892.e: A birch produces huge numbers of seeds. Only a few of them find a good place to grow.
80892.m: A birch produces lots and lots of seeds.

80893.q: What is good for looking at birch seeds, because they are so small?
80893.e: Birch seeds are only a few millimetres big. With a magnifying glass you can see their shape much better.
80893.m: With a magnifying glass you can discover small things.

80894.q: What do larch cones look like?
80894.e: Larch cones are small, egg-shaped cones with rounded scales. They look like little wooden roses.
80894.m: Larch cones are small and egg-shaped.

80895.e: Larch seeds have a little wing. The wind carries them away from the cone.
80895.m: Larch seeds fly on the wind.

80896.q: Which larch grows wild in the Swiss Alps?
80896.e: The European larch grows in the Alps. The Japanese larch is only sometimes planted in parks and plantations.

80897.q: What colour are young Swiss stone pine cones?
80897.e: Young Swiss stone pine cones are purple to bluish. When they are ripe, they turn brown.
80897.m: Young Swiss stone pine cones are purple.

80898.q: About how big is a Swiss stone pine nut?
a: As big as a hen’s egg
80898.e: Swiss stone pine nuts are about 1 centimetre big. They have a hard shell and a white kernel.
80898.m: Swiss stone pine nuts are as small as pips.

80899.q: Which mammal also likes eating Swiss stone pine nuts?
80899.e: Squirrels also take the nuts out of Swiss stone pine cones and make stores of them.
80899.m: Squirrels like Swiss stone pine nuts.

80994.q: Which bone is the strongest in the whole body?
80994.e: The thigh bone is very thick and strong. It carries a large part of the body's weight when you stand and walk.
80994.m: The thigh bone is the strongest bone in the body.

80995.q: How many thigh bones does a person have?
80995.e: There is one thigh bone in each leg. With two legs, that makes two.
80995.m: There is one thigh bone in each leg.

80996.q: Which two joints does the thigh bone connect?
80996.e: At the top, the thigh bone sits in the hip joint. At the bottom, it forms part of the knee joint.
80996.m: The thigh bone reaches from the hip to the knee.

80997.q: Which bone is the longest in your body?
80997.e: The thigh bone reaches from the hip to the knee. It is the longest bone in the whole body.
80997.m: The thigh bone is the longest bone.

80998.q: Roughly how long is the thigh bone compared with a person's height?
80998.e: The thigh bone is roughly a quarter as long as the whole person is tall.
80998.m: The thigh bone is about a quarter as long as the body.

80999.q: What is the round top end of the thigh bone that sits in the hip called?
80999.e: The top end is round like a ball. This head of the femur turns in a socket in the pelvis.
80999.m: The head of the femur is a ball in the hip joint.

81000.q: Which bone of the lower leg meets the thigh bone at the knee?
81000.e: In the knee joint, the thigh bone and the shin bone rest on each other. The shin bone is the thick bone at the front of the lower leg.
81000.m: The thigh bone and shin bone meet at the knee.

81001.q: What shape is the thigh bone?
81001.e: The thigh bone is a long bone. It is long and hollow inside like a tube.
81001.m: The thigh bone is a long, tube-shaped bone.

81002.q: What are the ribs attached to at the back?
81002.e: Each rib is connected to the spine at the back. From there it curves round to the front.
81002.m: At the back, the ribs are attached to the spine.

81003.q: Apart from the lungs, which important organ do the ribs protect?
81003.e: The heart is in the chest between the two lungs. The ribs surround it and protect it.
81003.m: The ribs protect the heart too.

81004.q: What do you call the ribs, breastbone and chest vertebrae together?
81004.e: The ribs, breastbone and chest vertebrae together form a cage of bones. That is why it is called the ribcage.
81004.m: The ribs, breastbone and chest vertebrae form the ribcage.

81005.q: What does your ribcage do when you breathe in deeply?
81005.e: When you breathe in, muscles lift the ribs. This makes the ribcage wider, and the lungs have room for air.
81005.m: When you breathe in, your ribcage gets wider.

81006.q: What are the front ends of many ribs made of so that they can bend?
81006.e: At the front, many ribs turn into cartilage. Cartilage is firm but bendy, so the ribcage can move when you breathe.
81006.m: Rib cartilage makes the ribcage bendy.

81007.e: The ribs are long, curved bones. They curve from the spine round the body to the front.

81008.q: What do the ribs form round the heart and lungs?
81008.e: The ribs lie side by side like the bars of a cage. That way they protect the organs in the chest from knocks.
81008.m: The ribs form a cage to protect the organs.

a: Between the breastbone and the shoulder
Between the knee and the foot
81009.e: The collarbone is at the top front of the chest. It reaches from the breastbone to the shoulder.
81009.m: The collarbone reaches from the breastbone to the shoulder.

81010.q: How many collarbones does a person have?
81010.e: There is a collarbone on each side, so one on the left and one on the right.
81010.m: Everyone has a collarbone on the left and on the right.

81011.e: The collarbone is a long bone that curves slightly like an S.

81012.q: Which bone breaks especially often in children, for example when they fall on their shoulder?
81012.e: A broken collarbone is one of the most common fractures in children. It often happens when they fall off a bike or while playing.

81013.q: What does the collarbone connect to the trunk?
81013.e: The collarbone connects the shoulder to the breastbone. Through this connection, the arm is attached to the trunk.
81013.m: The arm is connected to the trunk through the collarbone.

81014.q: Which bones can you feel on the left and right directly below your neck?
81014.e: The collarbones are at the top front of the chest, directly under the skin. That is why you can feel them easily below your neck.
81014.m: The collarbones are below the neck.

81015.e: The collarbone is a long, hard bone. It reaches from the breastbone to the shoulder.

81016.q: Where can you easily feel the collarbone with your fingers?
a: Under the skin at the top of the chest
At the back of the head
In the sole of the foot
81016.e: The collarbone lies directly under the skin. That is why you can easily feel it at the front below the neck.
81016.m: You can easily feel the collarbone below the neck.

a: At the front of the knee
At the back of the heel
At the side of the hip
81017.e: The kneecap is a flat bone at the front of the knee joint. You can feel it easily.
81017.m: The kneecap is at the front of the knee.

81018.e: The kneecap sits like a little shield in front of the knee joint. It protects it, for example, when you fall over.
81018.m: The kneecap is a shield for the knee.

81019.q: What is the technical name for the kneecap?
81019.e: Doctors call the kneecap the patella. It is Latin and means little dish.
81019.m: The technical name for the kneecap is patella.

81020.e: The kneecap is a small, flat bone at the front of the knee. You can feel it with your fingers.

81021.q: What is a newborn baby's kneecap still made of?
81021.e: In newborns, the kneecap is still soft cartilage. It only turns into bone in the first years of life.
81021.m: Babies have a kneecap made of cartilage.

81022.q: What happens when the doctor taps just below the kneecap with a little hammer?
81022.e: This is a reflex. The lower leg moves by itself, without you wanting it to.
81022.m: Tapping below the kneecap triggers a reflex.

81023.q: Which leg movement does the kneecap help with?
81023.e: The kneecap works like a lever for the thigh muscle. That way you can straighten your leg more powerfully.
81023.m: The kneecap helps you straighten your leg.

81024.q: What does the kneecap feel like when you touch it with your leg relaxed?
81024.e: With your leg relaxed, you can push the kneecap back and forth a little. But it is a hard bone.
81024.m: With a relaxed leg, the kneecap can be moved a little.

a: At the bottom end of the spine
At the top of the neck
At the front of the chest
81025.e: The tailbone is the very lowest piece of the spine. It is just above your bottom.
81025.m: The tailbone is the lowest piece of the spine.

81026.q: Where on the body is the tailbone?
a: Right at the bottom of the spine
At the front of the chest
At the back of the knee
81026.e: The tailbone is the lowest piece of the spine. It is at the back, just above your bottom.
81026.m: The tailbone is the lowest piece of the spine.

81027.q: According to scientists, what is the tailbone left over from?
81027.e: Many vertebrates have a tail in this place. In humans, only the small tailbone is left.
81027.m: The tailbone is what is left of a tail.

81028.q: When does the tailbone often hurt?
81028.e: If you fall on your bottom on the ice, for example, you can easily bruise your tailbone. It can hurt for some time.
81028.m: If you fall on your bottom, your tailbone can hurt.

81029.q: Which bone is directly above the tailbone?
81029.e: Above the tailbone is the sacrum. The sacrum is also made of vertebrae that have grown together.
81029.m: The sacrum is above the tailbone.

81030.q: How big is the tailbone compared with other bones?
81030.e: The tailbone is only a few centimetres long. It is much smaller than, for example, the pelvis.
81030.m: The tailbone is a small bone.

81031.q: Roughly what shape is the tailbone?
81031.e: The tailbone gets narrower and narrower towards the bottom. That is why it looks roughly like a small triangle with the point at the bottom.

a: At the front in the middle of the chest
At the top of the head
81032.e: The breastbone is a flat bone at the front in the middle of the chest. You can feel it easily.
81032.m: The breastbone is at the front in the middle of the chest.

81033.q: What is the little point at the bottom end of the breastbone called?
81033.e: The breastbone is said to look like a sword. Its lower tip is called the xiphoid process, which means ‘sword-shaped’.
81033.m: The lower tip of the breastbone is called the xiphoid process.

81034.q: Which organ is behind the breastbone?
81034.e: The heart is in the chest behind the breastbone, a little more to the left. The breastbone protects it from the front.
81034.m: The breastbone protects the heart from the front.

81035.q: What do you press on during chest compressions?
81035.e: During chest compressions, you press with your hands on the breastbone in the middle of the chest. This pumps blood through the body.
81035.m: During chest compressions you press on the breastbone.

81036.q: Where can you feel your breastbone with your fingers?
a: At the front in the middle of the chest
At the back of the neck
At the side of the hip
81036.e: The breastbone is directly under the skin at the front in the middle of the chest. That is why you can feel it easily.
81036.m: You can feel the breastbone on the front of the chest.

81037.q: How many parts does the breastbone have?
81037.e: The breastbone has three parts: the handle at the top, the body in the middle and the xiphoid process at the bottom.

81038.e: The breastbone is a flat, long bone. It is about as long as a hand.
81038.m: The breastbone is a flat, long bone.

81039.q: What is attached to the breastbone on both sides with cartilage?
81039.e: On the left and right of the breastbone, many ribs are attached by cartilage. In this way they form the front of the ribcage.
81039.m: Many ribs are attached to the breastbone at the front.

81040.q: Which large bone of the head can move?
81040.e: The bones of the skull are firmly joined together. Only the lower jaw can move, thanks to a joint.
81040.m: The lower jaw is the only large movable bone of the head.

81041.q: What do you need your lower jaw for?
81041.e: When you chew and speak, your lower jaw moves up and down. Without it you could not bite.
81041.m: You chew and speak with your lower jaw.

81042.q: What sits in the lower jaw?
81042.e: The lower teeth have their roots in the lower jaw. The upper teeth sit in the upper jaw.
81042.m: The lower teeth sit in the lower jaw.

81043.q: Where is the jaw joint that you can feel when you chew?
a: At the back of the neck
81043.e: If you put your fingers in front of your ears and open your mouth, you can feel the jaw joint move.
81043.m: The jaw joint is just in front of the ear.

81044.q: Which is the largest and strongest bone in the face?
81044.e: The lower jaw is bigger and stronger than all the other bones of the face. It has to withstand a lot when you bite.
81044.m: The lower jaw is the strongest bone in the face.

81045.q: What shape is the lower jaw when you look at it from above?
81045.e: The lower jaw is curved at the front and has two ends at the back. That makes it look like a horseshoe.
81045.m: The lower jaw is shaped like a horseshoe.

81046.q: What is the front part of the lower jaw that you can see at the bottom of the face called?
81046.e: At the front, the lower jaw comes together in the chin. You can feel the chin easily.
81046.m: The chin is the front part of the lower jaw.

81047.q: How does the lower jaw move when you open your mouth wide?
81047.e: When you open your mouth, the lower jaw drops down. The upper jaw stays fixed to the skull.
81047.m: When you open your mouth, the lower jaw drops down.

81048.q: What are the individual bones of the spine called?
81048.e: The spine is made of many individual bones stacked on top of each other. These bones are called vertebrae.
81048.m: The spine is made of many vertebrae.

81049.q: How many neck vertebrae does a person have?
81049.e: There are seven vertebrae in the neck. They make the neck flexible so that you can turn and nod your head.

81050.q: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have, despite its long neck?
81050.e: Almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae. In the giraffe, each single neck vertebra is simply very long.
81050.m: Even the giraffe has only seven neck vertebrae.

81051.q: What runs through a hole in the middle of the vertebrae?
a: A blood vessel to the foot
81051.e: The holes in the vertebrae together form a channel. In it lies the protected spinal cord, which carries messages from the brain to the body.
81051.m: The vertebrae protect the spinal cord.

81052.q: What is the top vertebra, which carries the head, called?
81052.e: The top neck vertebra is called the atlas. It is named after a giant from a Greek legend who holds up the sky.
81052.m: The top vertebra is called the atlas.

81053.q: What lies between the vertebrae and cushions knocks?
81053.e: Between most vertebrae there is a disc. It is like a little cushion and absorbs knocks.
81053.m: Discs lie like cushions between the vertebrae.

81054.q: What shape is the spine when you look at it from the side?
81054.e: From the side, the spine curves gently several times. This double S shape absorbs knocks when you walk and jump.
81054.m: From the side, the spine has a double S shape.

81055.q: What do you call animals that have a spine?
81055.e: Animals with a spine are called vertebrates. They include, for example, fish, birds, dogs and humans too.
81055.m: Animals with a spine are called vertebrates.

81056.e: The lumbar vertebrae are in the lower back between the ribcage and the pelvis. They are the thickest vertebrae because they carry a lot.
81056.m: The lumbar vertebrae are in the lower back.

81057.q: What is the technical term for a broken bone?
81057.e: Doctors call a broken bone a fracture. The word comes from the Latin word for break.
81057.m: The technical term for a broken bone is fracture.

81058.q: What happens to a broken bone if it is kept still?
81058.e: Bones are alive. They can make new bone where they broke and so grow back together.
81058.m: A broken bone can grow back together.

81059.q: Roughly how long does it take for a simple broken bone to heal in a child?
81059.e: A bone needs time to grow back together. In children this usually takes a few weeks.
81059.m: A broken bone needs a few weeks to heal.

81060.q: In whom do broken bones usually heal faster?
81060.e: Children are still growing and their bones have a good blood supply. That is why their fractures usually heal faster than in adults.
81060.m: Broken bones usually heal faster in children.

81061.q: What do you call a fracture in children in which the bone bends like a fresh twig?
81061.e: Children's bones are bendier. Sometimes they only crack on one side, like a young green twig. This is called a greenstick fracture.
81061.m: A greenstick fracture bends like a fresh twig.

81062.q: What do you call a fracture in which the skin is also injured and there is a wound?
81062.e: In an open fracture, the skin over the break is injured. Germs can then get into the wound.
81062.m: In an open fracture, the skin is injured too.

81063.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland for an ambulance?
81063.e: In Switzerland you reach the ambulance service on 144. 117 is the police and 118 the fire brigade.
81063.m: In Switzerland you call an ambulance on 144.

81064.q: What should you do with a part of the body that might be broken?
a: Move it as little as possible
Swing it back and forth quickly
81064.e: A broken bone should stay still so that the broken pieces do not move. Then you get help.
81064.m: You move a broken part of the body as little as possible.

81065.q: How can you often tell that a bone might be broken?
81065.e: After a fracture, the area usually hurts a lot and swells up. Often you can hardly move that part of the body.
81065.m: Severe pain and swelling can be signs of a fracture.

81066.q: Why do you get a plaster cast after breaking a bone?
a: So that the bone stays still
So that you get warm faster
So that your skin gets tanned
So that you can run faster
81066.e: The cast holds the broken bone firmly in the right position. That way it can grow back together straight.
81066.m: A cast keeps the broken bone still.

81067.q: What do you do with plaster bandages before you wrap them round an arm?
81067.e: Plaster bandages are dipped briefly in water. Then you wrap them round the part of the body, and they go hard as they dry.
81067.m: Plaster bandages are made wet and then go hard.

81068.q: Instead of plaster, what material are many light casts made of today?
81068.e: Today there are casts made of plastic. They are lighter than plaster and harden quickly.
81068.m: Many modern casts are made of plastic.

81069.q: What must a cast made of real plaster usually not do?
81069.e: Real plaster goes soft again in water. That is why you have to protect it when you shower.
81069.m: A cast made of real plaster must not get wet.

81070.q: What is put under the cast to protect the skin?
81070.e: Under the cast go a tube of fabric and soft cotton wool padding. That way the hard plaster does not press on the skin.
81070.m: Under the cast, soft padding protects the skin.

81071.q: What does the doctor use to cut a plaster cast off again?
81071.e: The cast saw has a blade that vibrates quickly back and forth. It cuts the hard plaster but not the soft skin.
81071.m: A cast saw removes the cast safely.

81072.q: What actually is plaster before it is made into a cast?
81072.e: Plaster comes from gypsum, a mineral found in nature. It is ground up and heated to make a white powder.
81072.m: Plaster comes from a natural mineral.

81073.q: What do people often feel when they wear a cast for a long time?
81073.e: Under the cast the skin cannot breathe well, and you cannot scratch. That is why it often itches.
81073.m: The skin under a cast often itches.

81074.q: Which kind of picture lets a doctor see whether a bone is broken?
81074.e: X-rays pass through skin and muscles but hardly through bones. That way you can see the bones on the picture.
81074.m: An X-ray shows the bones in the body.

81075.e: The German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered the rays. In many languages they are still named after him.
81075.m: X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen.

81076.q: In which year were X-rays discovered?
81076.e: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered the rays in November 1895. Soon afterwards they were already being used in medicine.

81077.q: What colour are bones on an X-ray?
81077.e: Bones stop the rays. That is where the picture is light, while soft parts appear dark.
81077.m: On an X-ray, bones are light.

81078.q: Which part of the body can be seen on one of the first famous X-ray images?
81078.e: Shortly after his discovery, Röntgen took a picture of his wife’s hand. You can see her finger bones and her wedding ring.
81078.m: One of the first X-ray images shows a hand with a ring.

81079.q: Which famous prize did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen receive as the very first winner in 1901?
81079.e: The Nobel Prize was awarded for the first time in 1901. Röntgen received the prize for physics for his rays.
81079.m: Röntgen received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics.

81080.q: Why do you sometimes have to wear a heavy apron when having an X-ray?
a: To protect you from the rays
81080.e: X-rays can be harmful in large amounts. The apron contains lead or similar materials and keeps the rays away from other parts of the body.
81080.m: An X-ray apron protects you from rays.

81081.q: Can you see X-rays with your eyes?
81081.e: X-rays are invisible. You only see the image they create on a film or screen.

81082.e: Bone marrow is a soft tissue inside the bones. It is well protected by the hard outer layer of bone.
81082.m: Bone marrow is inside the bones.

81083.q: What colour is the bone marrow that makes blood?
81083.e: There is red and yellow bone marrow. Red bone marrow makes new blood.
81083.m: Red bone marrow makes new blood.

81084.q: What is yellow bone marrow mainly made of?
81084.e: Yellow bone marrow is mainly fatty tissue. In adults it fills many long bones.
81084.m: Yellow bone marrow is mainly made of fat.

81085.q: Who can be helped by a donation of blood stem cells from bone marrow?
81085.e: With blood cancer, the bone marrow no longer makes healthy blood. Healthy stem cells from a donor can help it make healthy blood again.
81085.m: A bone marrow donation can help people with blood cancer.

81086.q: In whom is almost all the bone marrow red?
81086.e: Babies have red bone marrow in almost all their bones. As we get older, much of it turns into yellow bone marrow.
81086.m: Babies have almost only red bone marrow.

81087.q: What does the inside of many bones, where the bone marrow sits, look like?
81087.e: Inside, many bones are not completely hard but have fine struts with gaps. It looks like a sponge.

81088.q: In which flat bone of the chest is there red bone marrow even in adults?
81088.e: Even in adults, the breastbone still makes blood. That is why bone marrow can be taken from there for tests.
81088.m: The breastbone has red bone marrow even in adults.

81089.q: Which cells that fight germs are made in the bone marrow?
81089.e: White blood cells are also made in the red bone marrow. They fight off bacteria and viruses.
81089.m: White blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

81090.q: What are bones called that are often put into soup because of their marrow?
81090.e: Marrow bones are beef bones with a lot of bone marrow. They give the soup flavour.

81091.q: What are the lowest ribs called, which are not attached to the breastbone at the front?
81091.e: The 11th and 12th ribs end freely at the front in the muscles of the belly wall. That is why they are called floating ribs.
81091.m: The lowest ribs are floating ribs.

81092.q: What do you often have to take off before an X-ray?
81092.e: Metal strongly blocks X-rays and shows up as a bright patch on the image. It could hide something important.
81092.m: Metal gets in the way on an X-ray image.

81093.q: Which cloth can you use in first aid to keep an injured arm still?
81093.e: A triangular bandage belongs in every first aid kit. You tie it into a sling in which the arm can rest still.
81093.m: A triangular bandage keeps an injured arm still.

81094.q: Why does a ball fall down when you let go of it?
81094.e: The Earth pulls all things towards itself. That is why a ball falls down when you let go of it.
81094.m: The Earth pulls everything towards itself.

81095.q: Why don't people in Australia fall off the Earth?
a: The Earth pulls everything towards itself everywhere
The wind always blows from above there
81095.e: The Earth is a ball and pulls everything towards its centre. So for everyone on Earth, down is where the ground is.
81095.m: Everywhere on Earth, gravity pulls towards the ground.

81096.q: What keeps the Earth in its orbit around the Sun?
a: A magnet in the Earth's core
81096.e: The Sun is huge and pulls on the Earth. That is why the Earth circles the Sun and does not fly away.
81096.m: The Sun's gravity keeps the Earth in its orbit.

81097.q: Why does the air stay around the Earth and not fly off into space?
81097.e: Air is also pulled by the Earth. So a layer of air stays around the Earth that we can breathe.
81097.m: Gravity holds the air around the Earth.

81098.q: Which body in our solar system has the strongest gravity?
81098.e: The more mass a body in space has, the more strongly it pulls. The Sun has by far the most mass in the solar system.
81098.m: The Sun has the strongest gravity in the solar system.

81099.q: What is another word for gravity?
81099.e: Scientists also call gravity gravitation. The word comes from the Latin word for heavy.

81100.q: On which planet would you be heavier than on Earth?
81100.e: Jupiter is the largest planet and pulls much more strongly than the Earth. There, gravity would pull you down more than twice as strongly.
81100.m: Gravity is stronger on Jupiter than on Earth.

81101.q: Why is it hard work to walk up a mountain?
81101.e: When walking uphill, you have to lift your body upwards against gravity. That takes a lot of strength.

81102.q: What happens to the speed of a stone that falls from a tower?
81102.e: Gravity pulls the stone down during the whole fall. That is why it gets faster and faster.
81102.m: A falling stone gets faster and faster.

81103.q: What is falling called when only gravity acts and there is no air slowing things down?
81103.e: In free fall, only gravity acts. Completely without air, it happens for example in space or in a tube with no air in it.
81103.m: In free fall, only gravity acts.

81104.q: According to legend, which scientist dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
81104.e: Galileo Galilei studied how things fall more than 400 years ago. Whether he really used the Tower of Pisa for this is not certain.
81104.m: Galileo Galilei studied how objects fall.

81105.q: What is the jump called in which you fall into the depths on a stretchy rope?
81105.e: In a bungee jump, you first fall freely, then the stretchy rope slows the fall. In Switzerland you can jump, for example, from the dam in the Verzasca Valley, which is about 220 m high.
81105.m: In a bungee jump, a stretchy rope slows the fall.

81106.q: Why is a fall from a great height more dangerous than from a small height?
a: You are going faster when you hit the ground
The air is colder higher up
The ground is harder further down
You get heavier as you fall
81106.e: From a great height, you have much more speed when you land. That is why the impact is much harder.
81106.m: The further you fall, the harder the impact.

81107.q: What do you often feel in your tummy when a drop tower at the funfair suddenly shoots downwards?
81107.e: When falling fast, your body suddenly feels very light. Many people feel a tingling in their tummy.
81107.m: When falling, you often feel a tingling in your tummy.

81108.q: Why does a ball roll down a hill by itself?
81108.e: On a slope, gravity pulls the ball diagonally downwards. That is why it starts rolling without anyone pushing it.

81109.q: Where does a ball land if you drop it in a train travelling smoothly and steadily?
81109.e: Before you let go, the ball is moving at the same speed as you and the train. That is why it falls straight down in front of your feet.
81109.m: In a train moving steadily, a ball falls just as in a train standing still.

81110.q: Roughly when did Isaac Newton live?
81110.e: Isaac Newton was born in 1643 and died in 1727. So that is more than 300 years ago.
81110.m: Isaac Newton lived more than 300 years ago.

81111.q: According to the story, what did Newton wonder when he saw an apple fall?
81111.e: Newton wondered why the apple always falls straight down and never sideways or upwards. This question got him thinking about gravity.
81111.m: A falling apple got Newton thinking.

81112.q: What did Newton realise about the apple and the Moon?
a: The same force acts on both
The Moon is a giant apple
Apples only fall at full moon
81112.e: Newton realised that the Earth's gravity pulls the apple down. The same force also keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth.
81112.m: Gravity pulls the apple and keeps the Moon in its orbit.

81113.e: Newton was a scientist. He worked mainly as a physicist and mathematician and was a professor at Cambridge.
81113.m: Isaac Newton was a physicist and mathematician.

81114.q: Does Newton's famous apple tree still exist today?
a: Yes, it still stands in England
No, it was only in a fairy tale
81114.e: An apple tree in the garden of the house in England where Newton was born is said to be this famous tree. It once fell over, but grew again from its roots.
81114.m: Newton's apple tree still stands in England today.

81115.q: Which instrument for observing the stars did Newton improve?
81115.e: Newton built a telescope with a mirror. Such reflecting telescopes are still built today.

81116.q: What did Newton show with a triangular piece of glass, a prism?
a: White light is made up of colours
81116.e: Newton sent sunlight through a prism. The light was split into the colours of the rainbow.
81116.m: White light is made up of many colours.

81117.q: What do you need a parachute for?
81117.e: Without a parachute, you would fall faster and faster. The parachute slows you down so much that you can land safely.
81117.m: A parachute makes a safe landing possible.

81118.q: What must a parachute have so that it slows you down well?
81118.e: A large surface has to push a lot of air out of the way as it falls. This slows the fall a lot.
81118.m: The larger the surface, the more the parachute slows you down.

81119.q: What are parachutes usually made of today?
81119.e: Parachutes are sewn from light, tear-proof synthetic fabric such as nylon. So they are light and still strong.
81119.m: Parachutes are made of light, strong fabric.

81120.q: Which famous artist drew a parachute more than 500 years ago?
81120.e: Leonardo da Vinci drew a pyramid-shaped parachute around the year 1485. Much later it was shown that it works.
81120.m: Leonardo da Vinci drew a parachute very early on.

81121.q: Which plant sends its seeds through the air on little parachutes?
81121.e: Dandelion seeds hang from fine hairs like from a parachute. So they fly far away on the wind.
81121.m: Dandelion seeds fly on little parachutes.

81122.q: What is the wing called that lets you glide through the air down from mountains in Switzerland?
81122.e: With a paraglider, you take off from a slope and glide through the air for a long time. This is very popular in the Swiss mountains.
81122.m: With a paraglider you can glide through the air.

81123.q: How does a skydiver open their parachute?
a: They press a button on their helmet
They blow it up with their mouth
They open a zip on their tummy
81123.e: The parachute is folded up in a backpack. When the skydiver pulls a handle, the parachute comes out and opens.
81123.m: A handle on the backpack opens the parachute.

81124.q: What do some very fast racing cars use a parachute for?
81124.e: Very fast racing cars open a brake parachute after the finish. The air in the parachute slows the car down.
81124.m: A brake parachute can also slow down a car.

81125.q: What happens to a skydiver just after the parachute opens?
a: They spin round in a circle
81125.e: The open parachute fills with air and suddenly slows the fall a lot. Afterwards the skydiver sinks slowly to the ground.
81125.m: An open parachute slows the fall sharply.

81126.q: Which falls more slowly through the air: a feather or a stone?
81126.e: The feather is light and has a large surface for its weight. So the air slows it down much more than the stone.
81126.m: A feather falls more slowly through the air than a stone.

81127.q: What is the slowing effect of air on falling things called?
81127.e: A falling object has to push the air aside. This slows it down; it is called air resistance.
81127.m: Air resistance slows down falling things.

81128.q: What happened when an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time on the Moon in 1971?
a: Both landed at the same time
81128.e: There is no air on the Moon that could slow things down. That is why the hammer and the feather fell at exactly the same speed.
81128.m: Without air, a feather and a hammer fall at the same speed.

81129.q: What happens if you screw a sheet of paper up into a ball and drop it?
a: It falls faster than a flat sheet
It falls more slowly than a flat sheet
81129.e: The paper ball has a much smaller surface than the flat sheet. So the air slows it down less.
81129.m: A small surface is slowed down less by the air.

81130.q: What is a space with no air at all called?
81130.e: If you pump all the air out of a space, you get a vacuum. The word comes from the Latin word for empty.
81130.m: A space without air is called a vacuum.

81131.q: Why do downhill ski racers ski in a deep crouch?
a: So that the air slows them down less
So that they feel less cold
So that they can see better
81131.e: In a crouch, the skiers offer less surface to the air. So the air slows them down less and they go faster.
81131.m: In a crouch, the air slows you down less.

81132.q: Why is cycling hard work in a strong headwind?
a: The air slows you down more
81132.e: With a headwind, the air flows against you. You have to use more force to push against it.
81132.m: A headwind slows you down when cycling.

81133.q: Why does a leaf float slowly and swaying from the tree to the ground?
a: The air slows down the light leaf
The leaf is heavier than a stone
The tree holds on to it
The Earth does not pull leaves
81133.e: A leaf is very light and flat. The air slows it down a lot and makes it sway to and fro.
81133.m: Light, flat things are slowed down a lot by the air.

81134.q: What do you use to measure how heavy someone is?
81134.e: On scales, your body presses down. The scales show how heavy you are.
81134.m: You measure how heavy something is with scales.

81135.q: Why do you press down on the scales when you stand on them?
81135.e: Gravity pulls your body down. That is why you press on the scales, and they can show your weight.
81135.m: Gravity presses you onto the scales.

81136.q: Which is heavier: a kilogram of feathers or a kilogram of stones?
81136.e: A kilogram is always a kilogram. The feathers just take up much more space than the stones.
81136.m: A kilogram of feathers is just as heavy as a kilogram of stones.

81137.q: In which unit is a person's weight usually given?
81137.e: Body weight is given in kilograms, kg for short. An 8-year-old child often weighs about 25 kg.
81137.m: Body weight is measured in kilograms.

81138.q: Why does a full school bag feel heavier than an empty one?
a: There is more in it, and the Earth pulls on it more strongly
The air presses harder on full bags
The straps get shorter as you fill it
81138.e: The more things there are in the bag, the more strongly the Earth pulls on it. That is why you have to hold a full school bag more firmly.
81138.m: The more there is in it, the heavier the bag.

81139.q: What happens to the spring of a spring balance when you hang something heavy from it?
81139.e: The heavy thing pulls the spring down. The heavier it is, the longer the spring gets.
81139.m: The heavier something is, the more it stretches the spring.

81140.q: What does a beam balance do when there is the same weight on both sides?
81140.e: On a beam balance, the heavier side goes down. If both sides are equally heavy, the beam stays level.
81140.m: With equal weight, a beam balance stays balanced.

81141.q: Which is heavier: a litre of water or a litre of air?
a: Air has no weight at all
81141.e: A litre of air weighs only about one gram. A litre of water weighs around a thousand times more.
81141.m: Water is much heavier than air.

81142.q: Is gravity on the Moon stronger or weaker than on Earth?
81142.e: The Moon pulls things much less strongly than the Earth. That is why everything on the Moon is much lighter.
81142.m: Gravity on the Moon is weaker than on Earth.

81143.q: How high can an astronaut jump on the Moon?
a: Just as high as on Earth
81143.e: The Moon pulls much more weakly than the Earth. That is why you can jump much higher there.
81143.m: On the Moon you jump much higher.

81144.q: How does a heavy rucksack feel on the Moon?
81144.e: The Moon pulls things much more weakly than the Earth. That is why a rucksack feels much lighter there.
81144.m: On the Moon everything feels much lighter.

81145.q: What do astronauts on the Moon need to breathe?
81145.e: There is almost no air on the Moon. That is why astronauts wear a spacesuit that gives them air to breathe.
81145.m: On the Moon you need a spacesuit to breathe.

81146.q: Why is gravity on the Moon weaker than on Earth?
a: The Moon is much smaller and lighter
The Moon is further from the Sun
It is dark on the Moon
81146.e: The more mass a body in space has, the more strongly it pulls. The Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth.
81146.m: The small Moon pulls more weakly than the big Earth.

81147.q: How does a stone fall on the Moon compared with on Earth?
81147.e: Because the Moon pulls more weakly, a falling stone speeds up more slowly there than on Earth. It takes longer to reach the ground.
81147.m: On the Moon things fall more slowly than on Earth.

81148.q: What does the Moon's pull do to the Earth's seas?
81148.e: The Moon pulls on the water of the seas. This makes the water level rise and fall regularly; these are the tides.

81149.q: What was the mission called that first landed people on the Moon in 1969?
81149.e: In July 1969, the Apollo 11 mission landed on the Moon. Two astronauts walked on the Moon's surface.
81149.m: With Apollo 11, the first people landed on the Moon in 1969.

81150.q: What do you call a person who flies into space?
81150.e: People who fly into space on a rocket are called astronauts.
81150.m: Someone who flies into space is an astronaut.

81151.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon, in 1969?
81151.e: Neil Armstrong was the first person to step onto the Moon, in July 1969. He was an astronaut from the USA.
81151.m: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.

81152.q: Where do astronauts today often live in space for months at a time?
81152.e: The International Space Station, ISS for short, circles the Earth. People often live and do research there for half a year.
81152.m: People live in space on the ISS space station.

81153.q: Why do astronauts wear a spacesuit outside in space?
a: It gives them air and protects them
81153.e: In space there is no air to breathe, and it is very hot or very cold. The spacesuit supplies them with air and protects them.
81153.m: A spacesuit protects astronauts in space.

81154.q: Why do astronauts on the space station have to exercise every day?
a: Otherwise their muscles and bones get weak
So that they do not get bored
81154.e: Without gravity, muscles and bones hardly have to work and get weaker. With daily training, astronauts keep them strong.
81154.m: Astronauts train every day so that their muscles stay strong.

81155.q: Which sport did the astronaut Alan Shepard play on the Moon in 1971?
81155.e: Alan Shepard had taken a golf club and two golf balls to the Moon. In his stiff spacesuit he hit the balls with only one hand.
81155.m: Golf has been played on the Moon.

81156.q: What happens to astronauts' height in space?
81156.e: Without gravity, the spine is not squashed together and stretches a little. Back on Earth they get shorter again.
81156.m: In space, astronauts get a little taller.

81157.q: How long does the International Space Station take to go once around the Earth?
a: About an hour and a half
81157.e: The ISS flies very fast. It circles the Earth in around 90 minutes, so about 16 times a day.
81157.m: The ISS circles the Earth in about an hour and a half.

81158.q: What happens to a pencil that an astronaut lets go of on the space station?
a: It falls quickly to the floor
81158.e: On the space station, everything falls around the Earth together with the station. That is why things seem to float.
81158.m: On the space station things float.

81159.q: Why do astronauts sleep in a sleeping bag fixed to the wall?
a: So that they do not float around
So that they do not get cold
So that they do not snore
81159.e: Without the fixed sleeping bag, the astronauts would drift through the station in their sleep. This way they stay in their place.
81159.m: Astronauts sleep in fixed sleeping bags.

81160.q: What shape does a drop of water take in weightlessness?
81160.e: Without gravity, the water pulls itself together into a round ball. Such water balls float freely through the station.

81161.q: How does the toilet on the space station work?
a: It sucks things away with a stream of air
It flushes with lots of water
It works just like on Earth
There is no toilet at all
81161.e: In weightlessness, nothing falls down. That is why the toilet sucks everything away with a stream of air.
81161.m: The toilet in space works with a stream of air.

81162.q: Why do astronauts on the space station often eat tortillas instead of bread?
81162.e: Breadcrumbs would float around in weightlessness and could get into equipment or eyes. Tortillas hardly make crumbs.

81163.q: How can you experience weightlessness on Earth for a few seconds?
a: In an aeroplane flying an arc
In a lift that is standing still
81163.e: On a parabolic flight, an aeroplane flies a steep arc. For about 20 seconds the people inside float.
81163.m: On a parabolic flight you can float for a short time.

81164.q: What shape is a candle flame in weightlessness?
81164.e: On Earth, warm air rises and stretches the flame upwards. In weightlessness this does not happen, so the flame is round.
81164.m: In weightlessness a flame burns in a round ball.

81165.q: Why are tools on the space station often fixed with Velcro or cords?
a: So that they do not float away
So that they do not rust
81165.e: A tool that you let go of in weightlessness drifts away. With Velcro or cords it stays close by.
81165.m: On the space station, tools are fixed so that they do not drift away.

81166.q: What do you jump over in the high jump?
81166.e: In the high jump, a bar rests on two stands. You try to jump over it without knocking it off.
81166.m: In the high jump you jump over a bar.

81167.q: What is the well-known technique called in which you jump backwards over the bar?
81167.e: The American Dick Fosbury made this technique famous in 1968. Today almost all high jumpers jump like this.
81167.m: In the Fosbury flop you jump backwards over the bar.

81168.q: What do you land on in the high jump?
81168.e: Behind the bar there is a big, thick mat. It catches the jumpers softly.
81168.m: In the high jump you land on a thick mat.

81169.q: Why does every high jumper come back down after the jump?
81169.e: At take-off, you give yourself momentum upwards. Gravity slows this momentum and pulls the jumper back to the ground.
81169.m: Gravity brings every jumper back to the ground.

81170.q: Roughly how high is the men's high jump world record (as of 2025)?
81170.e: Javier Sotomayor from Cuba jumped 2.45 m in 1993. In 2025 this record had still not been broken.
81170.m: The men's high jump world record is about 2.45 m.

81171.q: Which sport does the high jump belong to?
81171.e: The high jump is an athletics event. Running, the long jump and the shot put also belong to it.
81171.m: The high jump belongs to athletics.

81172.q: In which kind of jump do athletes get much higher than in the high jump?
81172.e: In the pole vault, a bendy pole helps to fling the body high up. The best manage over 6 m.
81172.m: With a pole you jump much higher than without.

81173.q: What happens if the bar falls down in the high jump?
81173.e: The bar must stay in place after the jump. If it falls down, the attempt does not count.
81173.m: If the bar falls, the jump does not count.

81174.q: Why does the water in a waterfall plunge downwards?
81174.e: Gravity pulls the water down. Where there is a rock step, it plunges down.
81174.m: Gravity makes the water plunge down.

81175.q: What is the famous big waterfall near Schaffhausen called?
81175.e: At the Rhine Falls, the Rhine plunges over a wide rock step. It is one of the largest waterfalls in Europe.
81175.m: The Rhine Falls are near Schaffhausen.

81176.q: Which valley in the Bernese Oberland has especially many waterfalls, for example the Staubbach Falls?
81176.e: In the Lauterbrunnen Valley, many streams plunge over the steep rock walls. The Staubbach Falls drop almost 300 m.
81176.m: The Lauterbrunnen Valley is famous for its waterfalls.

81177.q: Which waterfalls near Lauterbrunnen plunge down inside a mountain?
81177.e: The Trümmelbach Falls flow through gorges and caves inside the mountain. They carry meltwater from glaciers into the valley.
81177.m: The Trümmelbach Falls plunge down inside the mountain.

81178.q: In which country is the highest waterfall in the world, Angel Falls?
81178.e: Angel Falls is in Venezuela in South America. There the water falls almost 1000 m.
81178.m: The highest waterfall in the world is in Venezuela.

81179.q: On which lake in the Bernese Oberland do the Giessbach Falls plunge down in 14 steps?
81179.e: The Giessbach Falls flow down in 14 steps into Lake Brienz. There is also a well-known old hotel there.
81179.m: The Giessbach Falls plunge into Lake Brienz.

81180.e: A plumb bob is a heavy, pointed weight hanging from a string.
81180.m: A plumb bob is a weight on a string.

81181.q: What do bricklayers use a plumb bob for?
a: To check whether a wall is vertical
81181.e: The string of the plumb bob hangs exactly vertically. If you hold it next to a wall, you can see whether the wall is straight.
81181.m: With a plumb bob you check whether something is vertical.

81182.q: Which way does the string of a plumb bob point when it hangs still?
81182.e: When the plumb bob hangs still, the string points exactly straight down towards the Earth.
81182.m: The string of a plumb bob points straight down.

81183.q: Why does a plumb bob always hang straight down?
a: Gravity pulls the weight towards the Earth
81183.e: The Earth pulls the heavy weight towards itself. That is why the string points exactly towards the centre of the Earth.
81183.m: Gravity pulls the plumb bob down.

81185.q: What did sailors in the past use a lead weight on a long line for?
a: To measure the depth of the water
81185.e: The sailors lowered the heavy weight into the water until it touched the bottom. From the line they could see how deep the water was.
81185.m: With a weight on a line you measure the depth of the water.

81187.q: What do you call a line that points in exactly the same direction as the string of a plumb bob?
81187.e: The string of the plumb bob points straight down. Every line in this direction is a vertical.
81187.m: The string of a plumb bob forms a vertical line.

a: Flashes from a thunderstorm far away
81286.e: With heat lightning, you see the light of flashes that are very far away. They are completely normal thunderstorm flashes.
81286.m: Heat lightning comes from a distant thunderstorm.

81287.q: Why do you hear no thunder with heat lightning?
a: The storm is too far away
The wind blows the thunder away
81287.e: The sound of thunder does not travel as far as the light of the lightning. That is why you only see the flashes.
81287.m: You see distant light, but you do not hear distant thunder.

81288.q: When do we often see heat lightning in Switzerland?
81288.e: In Switzerland, thunderstorms happen mainly in summer. In the evening you can see their distant flashes well in the dark sky.
81288.m: You often see heat lightning on summer evenings.

81289.q: From what distance can you usually no longer hear a storm's thunder?
81289.e: You can usually only hear thunder up to about 15 to 20 kilometres away. You can see the light of lightning much further.

81290.q: With heat lightning, what do you often see instead of the flash itself?
a: The glow reflected in the clouds
81290.e: The flash itself is often hidden behind clouds or the horizon. You then only see the clouds light up briefly.
81290.m: With heat lightning, often only the clouds light up.

81291.q: Why do you mainly see heat lightning at night?
a: The faint glow stands out in the dark
The moon makes the clouds glow
81291.e: The distant glow is faint. In bright daylight you hardly see it, but in the dark night sky you see it well.
81291.m: You see heat lightning best in the dark.

81292.q: Where in the sky do you usually see heat lightning?
81292.e: The thunderstorm is far away. That is why it lights up low on the horizon.
81292.m: Heat lightning usually flickers on the horizon.

81293.q: What should you do if you suddenly hear thunder after seeing heat lightning?
a: Find shelter in a house or car
81293.e: If you can hear thunder, the storm is already close enough for lightning to strike. Then you find shelter at once.
81293.m: If you hear thunder, find shelter.

a: Rain with small grains of ice
81294.e: In drizzle, lots of tiny droplets fall. You hardly feel them one by one.
81294.m: Drizzle is made of very fine drops.

81295.q: How big are the droplets in drizzle?
81295.e: Drizzle droplets are tiny. Normal raindrops are usually much bigger.

81296.q: What does the sky usually look like when it is drizzling?
81296.e: Drizzle usually falls from a flat, grey layer of cloud that hangs low over the land.
81296.m: When it drizzles, the sky is grey.

81297.q: How do drizzle droplets fall compared with big raindrops?
81297.e: Small droplets are light and are strongly slowed down by the air. They almost float down.
81297.m: The smaller a drop is, the more slowly it falls.

81298.q: How long can it drizzle in Switzerland?
a: Only during a flash of lightning
81298.e: It can drizzle for a long time from a thick, low layer of cloud. Sometimes it does not stop for hours.
81298.m: Drizzle can last a very long time.

81300.q: How much water does drizzle usually bring?
81300.e: Because the droplets are so small, drizzle usually only adds up to a little water.
81300.m: Drizzle usually brings only a little water.

81301.q: How does drizzle feel on your skin?
81301.e: The droplets are so fine that you can hardly feel more than a damp breath of air.

81302.q: How hot does a flash of lightning get?
81302.e: A flash of lightning heats the air to about 30,000 degrees. That is much hotter than the surface of the sun.
81302.m: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun.

81303.q: How long does a flash of lightning last?
81303.e: A flash of lightning only lasts a fraction of a second. Sometimes it flickers several times in quick succession.
81303.m: Lightning is over in a flash.

81304.q: What should you do if a thunderstorm comes while you are swimming?
a: Get out of the water at once
81304.e: In the water you are the highest point, and water conducts electricity. That is why you must get out at once in a thunderstorm.
81304.m: In a thunderstorm, get out of the water at once.

81305.q: Roughly how often a year does lightning strike the transmitter tower on the Säntis?
81305.e: The tall tower on the Säntis strongly attracts lightning. Scientists measure the strikes there.
81305.m: Lightning can strike the same place very often.

81306.q: Why are you fairly safe in a car during a thunderstorm?
a: The metal body carries the current round the outside
The rubber tyres protect you from the current
81306.e: The current flows over the car's metal body into the ground. Inside you are protected as long as you do not touch anything metal.
81306.m: In a closed car you are protected from lightning.

81307.q: Why should you not stand under a lone tree in a thunderstorm?
81307.e: A lone tall tree is often the highest point for miles around. Lightning likes to strike there.
81307.m: Never stand under a lone tree in a thunderstorm.

a: Lightning heats the air in an instant
Two clouds bump into each other
81308.e: Lightning makes the air very hot in an instant. The air expands with a bang, and we hear that as thunder.
81308.m: Thunder is caused by the hot air of the lightning.

81309.q: You count 9 seconds between the lightning and the thunder. Roughly how far away is the storm?
81309.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. 9 seconds divided by 3 gives 3 kilometres.
81309.m: Count the seconds and divide by three to get the distance in kilometres.

81310.q: Why does thunder often rumble for a long time instead of just banging once?
a: The sound comes from many points along the long flash
Several clouds thunder one after another
The rain makes the bang louder
The wind carries the bang round in a circle
81310.e: A flash of lightning is often several kilometres long. The sound from the parts further away arrives later, so it rumbles for a long time.
81310.m: Long rumbling comes from the long path of the lightning.

81311.q: Which Germanic god of thunder is Thursday named after?
81311.e: Donar was the god of thunder for the Germanic peoples; in the north he was called Thor. Thursday is named after him.
81311.m: Thursday is named after the thunder god Thor.

81312.q: What is the name of the Norse god who makes thunder with his hammer?
81312.e: In the old legends from Scandinavia, Thor hurls his hammer. Then there is thunder in the sky.
81312.m: Thor is the thunder god of the Norse legends.

81313.q: What does it mean if the lightning and the crash of thunder come at the same time?
81313.e: If lightning and thunder come almost at the same time, the lightning is only a few hundred metres away.
81313.m: If it crashes straight after the lightning, the storm is very close.

81314.q: How long should you stay under shelter after the last thunder?
81314.e: Lightning can still strike even at the end of a thunderstorm. That is why you wait about half an hour after the last thunder.
81314.m: After the last thunder, wait another half hour.

81315.q: Can you hear thunder in Switzerland in winter too?
81315.e: Thunderstorms happen mainly in summer. But occasionally there is a thunderstorm in winter too, sometimes even while it is snowing.
81315.m: It can sometimes thunder in winter too.

81316.q: What is the scale called that divides wind into forces from 0 to 12?
81316.e: The Englishman Francis Beaufort invented this scale for sailors about 200 years ago.
81316.m: Wind strength is measured on the Beaufort scale.

81317.q: What is the very strongest wind, force 12, called?
81317.e: Force 12 is the highest level. A wind like this is called a hurricane and causes great damage.
81317.m: The strongest storm is called a hurricane.

81318.q: What was the storm called that caused huge damage to forests in Switzerland on 26 December 1999?
81318.e: Lothar swept across Switzerland on St Stephen's Day 1999. It blew down millions of trees.
81318.m: Storm Lothar devastated many Swiss forests in 1999.

81319.q: What does a fast-flashing orange light on the shore of a Swiss lake mean?
81319.e: On many Swiss lakes, orange flashing lights warn of strong wind. The faster they flash, the more dangerous it is.
81319.m: Orange flashing at the lake warns of a storm.

81320.q: How does the orange light at the lake flash when a storm is coming?
81320.e: For a storm warning, the light flashes very fast, about 90 times a minute. For a strong wind warning it flashes more slowly.
81320.m: For a storm warning, the light flashes very fast.

a: A short, strong blast of wind
81321.e: In a gust, the wind suddenly becomes much stronger for a few seconds. Then it dies down again.
81321.m: A gust is a sudden blast of wind.

81322.q: How fast does the wind blow in a hurricane-force wind at least?
81322.e: From about 118 kilometres per hour, it is called force 12. That is as fast as a car on the motorway.
81322.m: A hurricane-force wind is as fast as a car on the motorway.

81323.q: Why should you not go into the forest during a storm?
a: Branches and trees can fall down
81323.e: Strong wind can tear off branches and blow down whole trees. That is why the forest is dangerous in a storm.
81323.m: Stay out of the forest in a storm.

81324.q: What should you do on a lake when there is a storm warning?
a: Go back to the shore at once
Go far out onto the lake
81324.e: A storm makes high waves and can tip boats over. That is why you head back to the shore at once when there is a warning.
81324.m: When there is a storm warning, go back to the shore at once.

81325.q: Are there two snowflakes that look exactly the same?
a: Yes, they all look the same
81325.e: Every snowflake grows a little differently on its way through the cloud. That is why none is exactly like another.

a: The many ice crystals reflect the light
81326.e: The many tiny crystal faces reflect all the colours of light. Together, that looks white to us.
81326.m: Snow is white because it reflects all the light.

81327.q: Why is it so quiet outside after fresh snow has fallen?
81327.e: There is a lot of air between the snowflakes. That is why fresh snow soaks up sounds like a sponge.
81327.m: Fresh snow makes the world quiet.

81328.e: Snowflakes grow high up in cold clouds. When they are heavy enough, they fall down.

81329.q: What does an ice crystal start to grow around in a cloud?
a: A grain of sand from the beach
81329.e: Tiny specks of dust float in the air. Water vapour freezes onto them and a crystal starts to grow.
81329.m: A snow crystal grows around a speck of dust.

81330.q: In what weather do especially big snowflakes fall?
a: When it is just around zero degrees
81330.e: At just around zero degrees, the crystals are a little wet. They stick together into big flakes.
81330.m: Big flakes fall when it is just around zero degrees.

a: Little pellets of snow and ice
81331.e: Graupel is small, round grains. They fall from shower clouds, usually when it is cool.
81331.m: Graupel is little grains of snow and ice.

81332.e: Graupel pellets are as small as pinheads or small peas.
81332.m: Graupel pellets are only a few millimetres big.

81333.q: How is graupel different from hail?
81333.e: Hailstones are hard and can get big. Graupel is small and soft and can easily be squashed.
81333.m: Graupel is smaller and softer than hail.

81334.q: What do graupel pellets do when they land on a hard road?
81334.e: Graupel pellets are round and light. On hard ground they bounce like little balls.

81335.q: What kind of weather do graupel showers often belong to in Switzerland?
81335.e: In April, sun, rain and cold change quickly. Then there are often short showers with graupel.
81335.m: Graupel often comes with changeable April weather.

81336.e: Graupel is white and not see-through because there is a lot of air in the pellets.

81337.q: What does graupel form from in the cloud?
81337.e: In the cold cloud, tiny water droplets freeze onto snowflakes. This is how the white pellets form.
81337.m: Graupel forms from snow and frozen droplets.

81338.q: Does graupel usually damage cars and roofs?
a: Yes, it makes everything wet and rusty
81338.e: Graupel is light and soft. It falls more slowly than hail and so rarely causes damage.

a: A smooth layer of ice on roads and paths
81339.e: With black ice, a thin, smooth layer of ice covers the ground. It is very easy to slip on it.
81339.m: Black ice is a smooth layer of ice on the ground.

81340.q: When does black ice often form?
a: When rain falls on frozen ground
81340.e: If rain falls on ground that is colder than zero degrees, it freezes into ice at once.
81340.m: Rain on frozen ground turns into black ice.

81341.q: Why can you often hardly see black ice?
a: It is as clear as glass
It is only there at night
